# augmented brain: the full documentation

> Your brain, augmented with AI. augmented brain gives an AI assistant (Claude Code today) memory, a method and a guard. This file is every page of the documentation at https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/, in English, generated from the Markdown sources by scripts/build-guides.py.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/getting-started.html

# Getting started


## What it is

augmented brain gives your AI assistant a memory, a method and a guard. Today the
assistant is Claude Code.

- **A memory.** Your tasks, decisions, people and rules are kept as plain text files on
  your computer. Every new session starts by reading them, so you never explain the same
  thing twice.
- **A method.** Every piece of work is a task that goes from idea to closed in six
  phases. You can stop a task today and pick it up next week, in any session.
- **A guard.** Before Claude runs a command, augmented brain reads it. Pushing code,
  becoming root or writing a password is stopped. Touching production asks you first.

You do not learn new commands. You talk to Claude as usual: "new task…", "park it",
"where were we?".

It is free and open source (MIT). It is also beta: a version still being tested, though what you
have keeps working from one version to the next. What it cannot do yet is in
[Known limitations](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/limitations.html).

This guide is for starting from scratch, even if you have never opened a terminal. It
takes about ten minutes.

## What you need

- **A computer with Linux, macOS or Windows.** On a Mac, macOS 13 (Ventura) or later: see
  the Apple menu → About This Mac. On Windows, Windows 10 or 11. What changes on each
  system is in [Installing](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/install.html).
- **A paid Claude account**: Pro or above. augmented brain is free, but it works with
  Claude Code, and Claude Code is not in the free plan. The plans are at
  [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing).
- **Your computer's password**, in case something missing has to be installed.

## 1. Open the terminal

The terminal is a window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons. You only
need it to install.

- **On a Mac:** press `Cmd + Space`, type `Terminal` and press Enter.
- **On Ubuntu:** press `Ctrl + Alt + T`.
- **On Windows:** press the Windows key, type `PowerShell` and press Enter.

## 2. Paste the install command

Copy this line, on a Mac or Linux:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

Or this one, on Windows:

```powershell
irm https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
```

Paste it into the terminal (`Cmd + V` on a Mac, `Ctrl + Shift + V` on Ubuntu, a right
click on Windows) and press Enter.

## 3. Answer the installer

It asks a few questions. To accept what it suggests, just press Enter.

1. **The language.** English or Spanish.
2. **Whatever is missing**, if anything: git (keeps the history of your notes), Claude
   Code and the Claude desktop app. It tells you what each one is for before installing it.
   If you already had Claude Code but it is behind, it offers to update it. If Claude Code
   is missing, it also asks whether you have a paid plan; a no does not stop it.
3. **Open the Claude app now?** Say yes.

If it asks for your password, type it even though you see nothing: the terminal does not
show it, not even as asterisks. Press Enter when done.

On a Mac, if git is missing, a window opens to install Apple's developer tools. Click
**Install** and accept. It takes a few minutes; the installer waits and carries on by itself.

On Windows there is no password to type: when Git is installed, Windows shows a window
asking for permission. Click **Yes**.

## 4. Sign in to Claude

In the Claude app:

1. Sign in with your account.
2. Open the **Code** tab.
3. Click **+ New** and type "Hi".

Without choosing a folder, you work in your personal space. For the work one, pick the
folder `~/augmented-brain/work` with **Choose…**. A **space** is a separate drawer of
notes: [Spaces](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html) explains them.

No desktop app (on Linux without `apt`, or if you said no)? The installer offers to open
Claude in the terminal instead, in your work space. Next times:
`cd ~/augmented-brain/work && claude`.

## 5. Answer the interview

The first time, Claude introduces itself and asks six questions, one at a time, telling
you what each one is for: who you are, what you look after, how you want answers, what
must not be touched, which tools you use and who you work with. You can skip any of them.

At the end it shows what it saved and offers to set up the backup. Say yes: your notes go
to a private repository of yours, and losing the computer loses nothing.

## Your first week

Talk to it as usual. These phrases pay off from day one:

| You say | What it does |
|---|---|
| "New task: prepare Thursday's meeting." | Opens a task and asks what it needs to define it |
| "Park it, we carry on tomorrow." | Writes down where you stopped and what comes next |
| "Where were we?" | Lists your live tasks with their next step |
| "Let's carry on with Thursday's meeting." | Resumes the task where you left it, in any session |
| "Note this: call the insurance." | Puts it in the inbox, without opening a task |
| "We go with supplier B, it is cheaper." | Writes it in the task's journal, with the date |
| "Save that as a lesson." | What you learned gets a note of its own |
| "Close the task." | Closes it; it is never deleted |
| "Lucía is my boss, I call her Lu." | Saves her, and next time it knows who she is |
| "Why did we pick supplier B?" | Finds it in your notes and gives you the decision, with date and reason |

More phrases, grouped by what you want: [What to say to Claude](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/phrases.html).

## Words you will hear

- **Space:** a separate drawer, with its own notes and rules. There are two, `work` and
  `personal`. The folder you open Claude in decides which one you are in.
- **Task:** something with a start and an end. It goes through six phases, from idea to
  closed.
- **Area:** something you always look after (the website, the house, a team). It groups
  its tasks.
- **Inbox:** where loose ideas wait until you sort them.
- **Guard:** the check that stops a risky command, or asks you first.
- **Backup:** your notes, pushed to a private git repository of yours after every session.
- **Plugin:** the piece that connects augmented brain to Claude Code. The installer puts
  it in.
- **Panel:** a page in your browser to see and change everything without asking Claude.

## If something goes wrong

- **Claude does not introduce itself or run the interview.** Start a new session. If
  nothing changes, open the terminal and type `augmented-brain doctor`: it tells you what
  is missing and how to fix it.
- **The terminal cannot find a command** (`command not found`, or "not recognized" on
  Windows). Close the terminal and open another one: the new one finds the programs just
  installed.
- **The installer says it cannot download from GitHub, or you stopped it.** Nothing is
  half done: paste the command again (in a while, if GitHub is having trouble).
- **Claude asks you for a paid plan.** Claude Code needs Pro or above.
- **Something else.** See [Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html).

## Where to go next

- [Tasks](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/tasks.html): how a task moves, and how to park and resume it.
- [The guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html): what it stops, what it asks, and why.
- [The panel](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html): everything at a glance, in your browser.
- [Backup and restore](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html): so a lost laptop loses nothing.

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/install.html

# Installing


One command installs augmented brain and everything it needs, on Linux, macOS and
Windows. This page says what that command does on each system, where it puts things and
what is different on each one. New to the terminal? [Getting started](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/getting-started.html)
walks you through it.

## On every system

- **A paid Claude plan** (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise) or an Anthropic API key. augmented
  brain is free, but it works with Claude Code, and the free plan does not include Claude
  Code. The installer says so before installing it. Plans: [claude.com/pricing](https://claude.com/pricing).
- **No administrator or root.** The program goes in your own folder. Only installing
  something that is missing, like git, may ask for your password.
- **The installer asks first.** The language, then each missing piece, with what it is for.
  Press Enter to accept what it suggests.
- **It always ends the same way:** two spaces, `work` and `personal` (in Spanish, `trabajo`
  and `personal`), in `~/augmented-brain`, the Claude Code plugin installed, and the offer to
  open Claude.
- **Every download is checked.** The program comes from the project's latest release on
  GitHub, and its SHA-256 must match the release's list, or nothing is installed. When
  GitHub fails to hand it out, the installer tries three times, also through GitHub's
  API; if all fails, it says so and installs nothing.

## Linux

**You need:** a 64-bit PC or Arm (amd64 or arm64), `curl` or `wget`, and `sha256sum` or
`shasum` (all usual distributions have them).

**Install:** open a terminal (on Ubuntu, `Ctrl + Alt + T`) and paste:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

**What it does:**

1. **git**, if missing, with your system's package manager: `apt` (Ubuntu, Debian), `dnf`
   (Fedora), `pacman` (Arch) or `zypper` (openSUSE). It asks for your password.
2. **Claude Code**, if missing, with Anthropic's own installer, into `~/.local/bin`. If
   you have it but it is behind, it offers to update it (`claude update`).
3. **The Claude desktop app**, if you want it, **only on systems with `apt`** (Ubuntu,
   Debian and their family): from
   Anthropic's apt repository, which it adds for you; it asks for your password. On other
   distributions you use Claude in the terminal.
4. **The program**, into `~/.local/bin/augmented-brain`.
5. **The PATH:** it adds `~/.local/bin` to `~/.bashrc` with bash, `~/.zshrc` with zsh, or
   `~/.profile` otherwise, unless it is already there.
6. **The setup**, and the offer to open Claude.

**Where things go:** the program and Claude Code in `~/.local/bin`; the configuration in
`~/.config/augmented-brain` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/augmented-brain`); your notes in
`~/augmented-brain/<space>/notes`.

**Good to know:**

- After installing, **open a new terminal**: the one you used does not see the new PATH yet.
- To work without the app: `cd ~/augmented-brain/work && claude`.

## macOS

**You need:** **macOS 13 (Ventura) or later**, which Claude Code needs; see the Apple menu →
About This Mac. Apple silicon and Intel Macs both work. Homebrew is not needed.

**Install:** open the Terminal (`Cmd + Space`, type `Terminal`, Enter) and paste:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

**What it does:**

1. **It checks the macOS version first.** Older than 13, it says so and stops, before
   installing anything that would not start.
2. **git**, if missing, comes with **Apple's developer tools**. A Mac has a `git` command
   even without them, but it only asks you to install them: the installer looks past it.
   A window opens: click **Install** and accept. It takes a few minutes; the installer waits
   and carries on by itself.
3. **Claude Code**, if missing, with Anthropic's own installer, into `~/.local/bin`. If
   you have it but it is behind, it offers to update it (`claude update`).
4. **The Claude desktop app**, if you want it: with Homebrew when you have it, otherwise
   straight from Anthropic, with its signature checked. It goes to `/Applications`, or to
   `~/Applications` if you cannot write there.
5. **The program**, into `~/.local/bin/augmented-brain`.
6. **The PATH:** with zsh, the Mac's usual shell, in `~/.zshrc`. With bash, in
   `~/.bash_profile`, or in `~/.bash_login` or `~/.profile` if you already have one of them:
   the Mac's Terminal reads those, not `~/.bashrc`.
7. **The setup**, and the offer to open the Claude app.

**Where things go:** as on Linux: `~/.local/bin`, `~/.config/augmented-brain` and
`~/augmented-brain`.

**Good to know:**

- After installing, **open a new Terminal window**.
- In the app: **Code** tab, **+ New**. Without choosing a folder you work in your personal
  space; for work, **Choose…** and pick `~/augmented-brain/work`.

## Windows

**You need:** **Windows 10 or 11**, 64-bit PC or Arm. **winget**, Windows' own installer,
which Windows 11 and an up-to-date Windows 10 already have (if it is missing, it comes with
"App Installer" from the Microsoft Store). The PowerShell that comes with Windows is enough.

**Install:** open **PowerShell** (Start menu, type `PowerShell`, Enter) and paste, with a
right click:

```powershell
irm https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
```

**What it does:**

1. **Git for Windows**, if missing, with winget. **On Windows it is required**, not only for
   the history of your notes: it brings **Git Bash**, where Claude runs commands with the
   guard watching. Windows shows a permission window: click **Yes**.
2. **Claude Code**, if missing, with Anthropic's own installer, into
   `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`. If you have it but it is behind, it offers to update it
   (`claude update`).
3. **The Claude desktop app**, if you want it, with winget.
4. **The program**, into `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin\augmented-brain.exe`.
5. **The PATH:** it adds that folder to your user's PATH. Claude Code's own installer leaves
   that to you; this one does it.
6. **The setup**, and the offer to open the Claude app.

**Where things go:** the program and Claude Code in `%USERPROFILE%\.local\bin`; the
configuration in `%APPDATA%\augmented-brain`; your notes in
`%USERPROFILE%\augmented-brain\<space>\notes`.

**Good to know:**

- After installing, **open a new PowerShell window**: the old one, and the ones already
  open, do not see the new PATH.
- **Claude runs commands in Bash, not in PowerShell.** The guard reads the shell, not
  PowerShell, so it stops every PowerShell command and Claude uses Git Bash instead. You
  will see that block in Claude's messages: it is expected.
- **The app may ask to update itself** the first time ("needs the latest desktop app"):
  winget does not always have the very latest one. Click **Update**.
- To work without the app: `cd ~\augmented-brain\work; claude` (Windows PowerShell has no
  `&&`).

## Check a download

You do not need this to install. It is for whoever wants to be sure that what they
downloaded is what the project published, made from its public code.

Every release is built by GitHub from a commit of `main`, never on someone's computer,
and GitHub signs a record of it: which workflow built each file, from which commit.
With the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) (`gh`), check any file of a release,
the installer included:

```bash
gh attestation verify augmented-brain_0.23.0-beta_linux_amd64.tar.gz -R icalvete/augmented-brain
```

It ends with `Verification succeeded!` and names the workflow and the commit. A file
changed after it was built fails.

`checksums.txt`, in every release, holds the SHA-256 of each archive and of both
installers. The installers check the archive against it; you can check any file too:

```bash
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt
```

The build is reproducible: the same commit, built with the Go version in `go.mod`, gives
the same bytes. `scripts/release-build.sh <version>` from a clone of that tag writes
the same `checksums.txt` as the release.

## Updating

When a new version is out, Claude tells you at the start of a session and offers to
update it. You can also do it yourself:

```bash
augmented-brain update
```

It updates the program and the Claude Code plugin. Before, it checks the installation
(and shows what fails) and backs up every space that has a backup; if a backup fails,
it updates nothing (`--force` updates anyway). If no space has a backup, it says that it
goes ahead with no copy to go back to. After, it restarts the idle sessions that still run the old version, with the same
conversation, and says which are left and which task each space has active: ask those
sessions to park their task. Running the install command again also
updates, without those steps. `augmented-brain update --plugin` updates only the plugin.

It first asks GitHub for the latest version, once: if GitHub does not answer, it says so
and stops. The download is then tried three times, also through GitHub's API. If it still
fails, or the program is not the new version afterwards, it says so and ends with an
error: nothing changed, run it again later.

Then close and open the sessions it could not restart (one that was answering, or on
Windows those of Claude Desktop). A session that was open keeps the old program until it restarts,
and its augmented brain tools may fail. `augmented-brain doctor` and the start of a new
session tell you how many sessions still run the old version.

Your notes and settings stay as they are. Sometimes a new version stores notes in a new
way. Then the first session moves them to the new way, after keeping a full copy in the
`migrations/` folder of the configuration, and Claude tells you. An older version never
breaks notes a newer one wrote: it refuses them and asks to be updated. So update every
computer you use.

## Uninstalling

```bash
augmented-brain uninstall
```

It shows what it will remove and asks. It removes the program, the Claude Code plugin and
what Claude Code keeps of it (its cache, its data and its server's logs).

- **First, what would keep running without it:** the [remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html) services
  and the sessions opened for tasks (`session start`). Without the plugin they would go
  on with no guard, and with no program left to take them away. If one cannot be
  stopped, nothing else is removed: it tells you why, so you can fix it and run it again.

- **Your notes stay** in `~/augmented-brain/`: they are yours. If you install it again,
  you find everything as it was.
- **The configuration stays** too. `--config` removes it, with your profile.
- **To start from scratch**, `--all` also removes every space's notes. First it shows each
  folder with how many notes it has, and asks. It removes only what augmented brain keeps
  there (the note folders, `MEMORY.md`, `inbox.md`, `docs/`, `archive/`), and the folder
  only if nothing else is left. Anything of yours inside a space's folder stays. A notes
  folder that holds a work folder, your home folder, or a folder with no notes is left
  whole, and the plan says so. `--config` only removes a folder that holds a
  `config.toml`. Your backup on GitHub is not deleted: it says which one it is and how to delete
  it. If a space has no backup, it warns you that its notes will be gone for good. To keep
  them, answer no and set up the backup first.
- Claude Code, its desktop app, git and the PATH entry stay: Claude Code lives in that
  same folder.

On Windows the program file disappears a moment after the command ends, because Windows
does not let a running program delete itself.

All the commands and their options: [Commands](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html).

## If something goes wrong

- **The terminal cannot find a command** (`command not found`, or "not recognized" on
  Windows). Open a new terminal: the one you used does not see the new PATH yet.
- **Anything else after installing.** Run `augmented-brain doctor`: it says what is missing
  and how to fix it. It also warns you when a space has no backup, when Claude Code keeps
  a second memory of its own for your spaces' folders, and when other users of the
  computer could read your notes. If the configuration is broken, it tells you how to go
  back to a version that worked.
- **"This system is not supported yet".** It works on Linux, macOS and Windows, on 64-bit PCs
  and Arm.
- **macOS: "Claude Code needs macOS 13".** Update the Mac in System Settings → General →
  Software Update, then paste the command again.
- **macOS: the developer tools window did not open.** Run `xcode-select --install` and then
  the install command again.
- **Linux: no desktop app offered.** It is only for systems with `apt` (Ubuntu, Debian
  and their family); use Claude in the terminal.
- **"cannot download … from GitHub".** GitHub is having trouble. Nothing was installed:
  paste the command again in a while.
- **You stopped the installer half way** (Ctrl+C, a closed window). Paste the command
  again: it sets everything up from the start.
- **Windows: "Git was not installed".** The installer tries winget first and then Git's own
  download. If both fail, install Git from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/download/win)
  and run the command again. The desktop app needs winget: update "App Installer" from the
  Microsoft Store.
- **Claude asks whether you trust the folder.** The first time you open Claude in a
  folder, Claude Code asks this before loading anything. Say yes in your work folder: until
  then, augmented brain cannot load your notes.
- **Windows: accents look broken (`sesiÃ³n`).** Windows PowerShell 5.1 misreads what
  other programs write when it captures it (a redirection, a remote session). The text is
  right: in Git Bash, or in a window, it shows well.
- **Claude asks for a paid plan.** Claude Code needs Pro or above.
- **Something else.** See [Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html), or tell us in
  [the project's issues](https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/issues), with what
  showed up on screen.

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html

# Spaces


You open Claude in `~/augmented-brain/work/website`. It sees your work tasks, your work
rules and the people from work. You open it in `~/augmented-brain/personal/blog`. Now it
sees your personal notes, and nothing from work.

That is a **space**: a full set of notes, rules and backup, kept apart from the others.
The installer creates two, `work` and `personal` (in Spanish, `trabajo` and `personal`).

## The folder picks the space

Each space has one or more **work folders**. When you open Claude inside one of them, you
are in that space. The space's notes live in a `notes/` folder inside it:

```
~/augmented-brain/
├── work/          a work folder: open Claude here for work
│   ├── notes/     the work notes
│   └── website/   a project of yours
└── personal/      and here for personal things
    └── notes/
```

The configuration file says which folders belong to which space:

```toml
# ~/.config/augmented-brain/config.toml
default_space = "personal"

[spaces.work]
memory = "~/augmented-brain/work/notes"
work_folders = ["~/augmented-brain/work", "~/code"]

[spaces.personal]
memory = "~/augmented-brain/personal/notes"
work_folders = ["~/augmented-brain/personal"]
```

`memory` is where the notes are. `work_folders` are the folders that pick the space.

To know which space a folder belongs to, run this in it:

```bash
augmented-brain space
```

## Outside every space

The desktop app starts each new session in a scratch folder of its own. That folder is
in no space. Then the **default space** is used, `personal` unless you change it, and
Claude tells you in one line, with how to switch to work.

The default space matters for one more thing: its backup carries your profile and the
shared notes. Set it with `default_space` in the configuration. With a single space, it
is that one.

## Your projects live elsewhere?

If your code is in `~/code`, add that folder to the `work_folders` of the right space, as
in the example above. Then opening Claude in `~/code/shop` uses the work space.

## Add a space

For a client, a side project or a volunteer job:

```bash
augmented-brain space add client
```

It asks for the work folder and the notes folder, suggesting
`~/augmented-brain/client` and `~/augmented-brain/client/notes`. Press Enter to accept.
If there was no default space yet, it sets one. The options are in
[Commands](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html#augmented-brain-space-add).

## What each space has, and what they share

Each space has its own:

- notes: tasks, areas, knowledge, people, inbox, reviews;
- rules, on top of the common ones;
- backup repository.

Every space shares:

- **your profile**: who you are and how you like to work. You are the same person at
  work and at home.
- **the shared notes**: rules, references and lessons that hold everywhere (below).
- **the guard's lists**: production AWS profiles, machines not to touch, the
  repositories where Claude may commit and those it must never touch, and the root
  exceptions. They hold on the whole machine. A production
  profile saved from the work space is guarded in the personal one too.

Spaces never read each other's notes on their own.

## A task of another space

Sometimes you decide, in one space, something about a task of another: in a personal
session you settle how a work task goes on. Say so, and Claude reads or writes that task
where it lives, in the other space. It can read it, list that space's live tasks to find
it, add to its journal, tick a step, and change its next step, status or who it waits
on.

- What Claude writes there ends in `(from personal)`, so whoever reads it in the other
  space knows where it was decided.
- Nothing is copied into this space's notes: what Claude reads stays in the
  conversation.
- Claude does it only when you ask, as with sending a capture to another space.
- Closing that task is done from a session of its own space, because closing also ends
  the task's session and its worktree.
- That space is backed up when this session ends, if it has a backup: it does not wait
  for a session of its own.

## Shared notes

Some things you learn hold everywhere: how git behaves, how you like answers, a lesson
about a tool. Saving them once per space would leave two copies that drift apart. So they
go once in the **shared notes**, next to your profile, in `shared/` inside the
configuration folder.

Only rules, references and lessons can be shared. Tasks and areas always belong
to one space. A person can be in several spaces, each with its own note and only what
you want visible there (see People in Notes).

You do not move files by hand. Tell Claude "this holds everywhere" and it saves the note
as shared. Every session loads the shared rules, and lists the shared references and
lessons for Claude to open when it needs them. They travel in the backup of the default
space, with your profile.

## Next

- [Tasks](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/tasks.html): what goes inside a space.
- [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html): every setting of a space.

# Tasks


You say "new task: move the blog to a new host". Claude opens a task. You agree on what
"done" means, then on a plan. In the evening you say "park it". Next week, in a new
session, you say "let's carry on with the blog", and Claude picks it up where you left it.

A **task** is any piece of work with a start and an end. It is one text file in the
space's `tasks/` folder.

## What a task looks like

```markdown
---
id: task-move-the-blog
type: task
title: Move the blog
area: area-blog
status: parked
waiting_on: me
next: Copy the database to the new host
created: "2026-10-15"
updated: "2026-10-16"
---
## Essentials
The blog moves to a cheaper host. Plan agreed: copy, test, switch the domain.
Done: the new host is ready. Next: copy the database.

## 3. Plan
- [x] Open an account on the new host
- [ ] Copy the database
- [ ] Switch the domain

## Journal
- 2026-10-15 — Task opened.
- 2026-10-16 — We go with the cheaper host: same speed, half the price.
- 2026-10-16 — Parked. Next: Copy the database to the new host
```

The part between the `---` lines is the **header**: the data the program reads. Below it
is free text, in any language. The first section is always the **essentials**: a few
lines that are enough to resume the task. The last one is always the **journal**: dated
lines of what happened.

You can open and edit the file with any editor. The full format is in the
[memory format](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html).

## The six phases

A task moves through six phases. **You approve each change of phase.** Inside a phase,
Claude works without asking at every step.

1. **Definition**: what we want, what is out, and how we will know it worked.
2. **Analysis**: how things really are, measured, not assumed.
3. **Plan**: ordered steps, each with how to undo it.
4. **Execution**: doing it, writing in the journal as we go.
5. **Validation**: proving the "done" criterion.
6. **Closed**: finished. It is kept, never deleted.

The phase is the task's `status`. Two more statuses pause a task without losing anything:

- **parked**: paused, to resume soon. `next` says exactly how.
- **someday**: not for weeks. It leaves the list Claude reads at the start, and stays in
  its area.

A small task may skip phases (straight from definition to execution): it is allowed, and
the journal says which phases it skipped. A closed task stays closed: closing it again is
refused, so its result is never written over, and opening it again needs a reason: Claude asks
you first, and the reason goes to the journal. In the panel, choosing a new status for a
closed task is that reason.

## Who it waits on, and what comes next

Every task says two more things:

- **waiting_on**: `me` (you), `nobody`, a person's name, or another task.
- **next**: the single next action, in one line.

That is what "where were we?" shows you: each live task, those waiting on you first, with
its next step.

## Park and resume

Before you switch to other work, say "park it". Claude writes down three things: the exact
next step, who it waits on, and the essentials, rewritten so another session can resume
without reading the whole journal.

To resume, say "let's carry on with the blog". Claude reads the task first. Then it checks
the real state of what the task touches (the files, the server) before trusting the note.
Things may have changed since.

## The journal, as you go

Each decision or finished step goes to the journal at the moment, not only when you park
it. A session can end at any time, and what is not in the note is lost.

If the session has a task open and nothing has been written in it for 20 minutes, Claude
gets a reminder at the end of its answer, once. Each session has its own task: with two
windows on different tasks, each is reminded of its own. When a long conversation is compacted (Claude
Code replaces the details with a summary), the summary is kept in `archive/sessions/`,
and the journal points at it. The summary can be wrong, so Claude is asked not to take it
as fact, to check before stating anything from before, and to tell you the session was
compacted and suggest parking the task and going on in a new session, which starts from
the notes.

### A long journal

A task that lasts weeks can gather a long journal, too long for Claude to read in one go.
When a task passes 24 KB, its oldest entries move to a file of their own in
`archive/journals/` (named after the task and the dates of the first and the last entry),
and one line in the journal says how many moved and where. About the last 8 KB of entries
stay in the task. Nothing is lost: the entries are moved as they were written, and Claude
reads that file when it needs something from back then.

## Steps and subtasks

A big task can be split in two ways.

A **step** is a small part: a checkbox in the task's Plan, such as `- [ ] Copy the
database`. Claude ticks it when it is done. The list of tasks shows how many are done
("1/3 steps").

A **subtask** is a part with a life of its own, because it waits on someone else or goes
at its own pace. For example, "Ask Diego for the domain password" waits on Diego, while
you go on with the rest. A subtask is a whole task, with one more line in its header:
`parent: task-move-the-blog`.

- Only one level: a subtask has no subtasks.
- The bigger task closes last, when all its subtasks are closed.
- Parking the bigger task leaves its subtasks as they are.

Rule of thumb: if it waits on someone or has its own pace, it is a subtask. Otherwise, it
is a step.

## Dates to look at something again

Some checks belong to a day: "on the 16th, is the certificate renewed?". Tell Claude and
it adds a **watch date** to the task. From 7 days before, and every day after, Claude
tells you at the start of the session, until it is marked done.

This also works on a closed task. Closing is often when you write down what to check
later, so when Claude closes a task that still has one, it tells you it will keep coming
up.

For something that is not a task ("remind me on Thursday to call the insurance"), Claude
uses the inbox instead: see [Areas, knowledge and the rest](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/notes.html#inbox).

## Closing

Say "close the task". Claude writes the result, and the task stays in its folder, marked
closed. Nothing is ever deleted.

A task that nobody has changed for 14 days comes up in the
[weekly review](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/weekly-review.html), so nothing stalls in silence.

## Next

- [What to say to Claude](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/phrases.html): the phrases for all of this.
- [MCP tools](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html): the tools Claude uses behind each phrase.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/notes.html

# Areas, knowledge and the rest


Tasks come and go. Around them, a space keeps a few other kinds of notes. Each one is a
Markdown file in its own folder, and you never have to create them by hand: you say it,
and Claude writes it.

## Areas

"The blog", "the servers", "the house". An **area** is something you look after with no
end date. It groups the tasks and the knowledge that belong to it.

You say: "the newsletter is a new area". Claude creates `areas/area-newsletter.md`. Its
body says what you look after, how it is going and what to watch. The program lists the
area's tasks and knowledge inside it by itself.

The first-session interview creates your first areas, from what you said you look after.

## Knowledge

What is worth keeping beyond one task. There are two kinds, in `knowledge/`:

- A **reference** says how something works: "how the blog is deployed".
- A **lesson** says what you learned, with a title that already states the conclusion:
  "Test the backup restore, not only the backup".

You say: "save that as a lesson". Both belong to an area, and Claude opens them when a
task needs them.

## People

You say: "Diego runs the hosting company; I call him Dieguito". Claude saves
`people/person-diego.md`. The next time you say "tell Dieguito it is done", it knows who
he is.

A **person** has a name, who they are to you, the other names you use for them, and
anything worth remembering. A task can wait on a person (`waiting_on: Diego`).

**The same person can be in more than one space.** Say Diego is your client and also
your friend. Each space keeps its own note for him, with the same id, and that note holds
only what you want to see there: his role, his other names and his details. The panel
joins them into one card, so you see everything about him in one place, and for each
detail you tick the spaces where it shows. A detail about your friend that you leave
unticked for `work` is never written in a work file, so it never reaches a work backup.
When you ask Claude to remember someone, it asks in which spaces they should be visible.

## Inbox

An idea that is not a task yet. You say: "note this: look at the new hosting prices".
Claude adds one dated line to `inbox.md`, without opening a task:

```
- 2026-10-17 — Look at the new hosting prices
- 2026-10-17 — Call the insurance (remind: 2026-10-22)
```

Each line is a **capture**. The [weekly review](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/weekly-review.html) empties the inbox: each
capture becomes a task, goes to an area or knowledge, or is dropped.

"Remind me on Thursday to call the insurance" is a capture with a date. From a week
before, and every day after, it comes up at the start of the session, until the weekly
review deals with it (or you mark it done in the panel).

## Rules

How you want Claude to work. You say: "from now on, answer in short sentences". Claude
saves it as a **rule**. Every session loads every rule, whole.

There are three levels:

- **common rules**, which come with the program: verify before advising, never push
  unless asked, never become root, never write secrets…
- **shared rules**, yours, for every space ("answer in short sentences");
- **space rules**, in the space's `rules/`, for what only applies there ("the database
  of the shop is never restarted on a Friday").

A rule that holds everywhere goes to the shared notes. Tell Claude "this holds
everywhere".

Your rules are read at the start of every session, so each one costs a little room every
time. `augmented-brain doctor` says how much they take, and which are the longest.

## Your profile

Who you are and how you like to work: your name, what you do, your language, how long
you like answers, how much Claude may do without asking. It is one file for every space,
`profile.md` in the configuration folder. The first-session interview writes it. To
change it, tell Claude.

## Repositories

What each of your git repositories is, one line each: "`~/code/blog` — The blog, built
with Hugo". It lives in one reference of the space, `knowledge/ref-repositories.md`, so
the backup keeps it. You write the line in the panel's Repositories page, or Claude
writes it for you.

## The index

`MEMORY.md` is the list Claude reads at the start of every session: your profile line,
the rules, the areas and the live tasks with their status and next step. The shared
references and lessons are listed by title and file. At the start, Claude gets it
shorter: tasks go without their summary, and a task shows its next step (its first 120
characters) only when it waits on you. Claude reads a task before working on it. The
program writes this file after every change: do not edit it by hand, it would be
rewritten.

## Documents and the archive

Two folders are never loaded:

- `docs/<task>/` keeps the long documents a task produces (a plan, an analysis), next to
  the notes and out of the project's repository.
- `archive/` keeps old things: long journals moved out, summaries of compacted
  conversations. Nothing there is ever deleted.

## Editing by hand

Every note is plain Markdown. Open it with any editor and change it. Afterwards, run
`augmented-brain check` in a folder of the space: it checks every note and rebuilds the
index.

## Next

- [What to say to Claude](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/phrases.html): the phrases for each kind of note.
- [Memory format](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html): every folder and header field.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html

# The guard


Claude is about to run `git push origin main`. Before it does, augmented brain reads the
command and stops it: pushing is for you. Claude tells you the change is ready, and you
push it yourself.

That check is the **guard**. It reads every command Claude runs, and every file it writes,
before it happens. It has three answers:

- **Go ahead**: almost always. `ls`, `go test`, `aws --profile dev s3 ls`.
- **Ask you**: Claude Code shows the command and waits for your yes. `aws --profile prod
  …`, `ssh db01 …`.
- **Stop**: the command does not run. Claude gets the reason, and what to do instead.

The reasons are in your language, the `language` of your
[configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html) (the system's while it cannot be read).

**The guard is a safety net against slips, not a security boundary.** It reads commands
as text. It catches the mistakes an assistant makes, also hidden inside other commands.
A program determined to get around it could. Read the
[disclaimer](https://github.com/icalvete/augmented-brain/blob/main/DISCLAIMER.md).

## What it stops

- **Commits and pushes.** `git commit`, `git push`, and what publishes like a push:
  `git subtree push`, `git send-pack`, `gh release create`, `glab release create`.
  Unless you let Claude in a repository (below). Asking for help passes: `git commit
  --help`, `gh pr merge --help`, `su --version`.
- **Becoming root.** `sudo`, `su` (and `sudo-rs`, `su-rs`), `doas`, `pkexec`, `run0`, `sudoedit`, `systemd-run`
  without `--user`, `ssh root@…`, a container given the whole machine (`docker run
  --privileged`, `-v /:/host`, `--pid=host`), and on Windows `gsudo` and `runas`. Claude
  gives you the exact command to run yourself. Running as another user (`sudo -u www-data …`) is fine.
- **Secrets.** A token or key written in a command or in a file Claude writes. Secrets are
  read from the system keychain, an environment variable or a secrets manager, never
  typed in.
- **Wiping your home folder or the whole disk.** `rm -r` of `~` or `/`, also after a
  `cd` (`cd ~ && rm -rf .`), and on Windows however the path is written.
- **PowerShell.** The guard reads the shell, not PowerShell, so it stops every PowerShell
  command, and `cmd` or `powershell` started from Bash too. Claude runs it in Bash (Git
  Bash on Windows) instead. You will see that block on Windows: it is expected.

## What it asks you first

- **Production.** An `aws` command with a profile you marked as production. It checks
  every profile the command may use: `--profile`, `AWS_PROFILE`, `AWS_DEFAULT_PROFILE`,
  or `default` when none is set. The same for tools that call AWS on their own: `cdk`,
  `sam`, `serverless`, `terraform`, `tofu`, `pulumi`, `eksctl`, `copilot`. And any other
  program with a production profile set in the command itself (`AWS_PROFILE=prod bash
  deploy.sh`): whatever it runs may reach AWS with it.
- **Machines not to touch.** `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync`, `sftp` and `mosh` to a host you marked
  as untouchable. `db01` and `db01.example.com` count as the same host.
- **Starting a release workflow by hand** (`gh workflow run release`, or the same
  through `gh api`). It publishes a version, so it is your call, but you do not need a
  terminal: say yes only if you asked for that release now. If you say no, or nobody
  answers, nothing starts. In `bypassPermissions` mode, where Claude Code may skip that
  dialog, it is stopped instead. Other workflows go on; one named only by its number
  asks too.
- **Pushes that rewrite history**, even where Claude may push: `--force`, `--delete`,
  `--mirror`, `--prune`, a refspec starting with `+` or `:`.
- **What it cannot read.** A program given as a variable (`$TOOL deploy`), commands
  nested too deep (more than four commands, one inside another: `sudo`, `ssh`, `bash -c`,
  `find -exec`, a git alias), a command longer than 256 KB, `rm -rf "$DIR/"*` with a
  variable that may be empty, an `rm -r .` after a `cd` it cannot follow, a script it
  cannot read or larger than 64 KB, a script that the same command writes in a way it
  cannot read and then runs (`curl -o x.sh … && sh x.sh`).
- **The guard's own settings.** Claude never changes augmented brain's configuration or
  Claude Code's settings on its own, since a line there could switch a check off.

## Let Claude commit in a repository

By default, Claude never commits or pushes. For a repository of yours where you want it
to, list it in the configuration, in any space:

```toml
[spaces.work]
git_allowed_repos = ["~/code/blog", "~/code/blog-*"]   # commit and push freely
git_ask_repos = ["~/code/shop"]                        # ask me each time
```

- Claude must name the repository in the command: `git -C ~/code/blog push`.
- A git worktree of a listed repository counts as it.
- `~/code/blog-*` covers every `blog-<name>` folder next to `blog`.
- A repository in both lists asks.
- The lists of every space count together: a repository is yours, not the space's.

The easiest way is the panel's **Guard** page. Adding a repository to the list where
Claude commits and pushes without asking shows a warning, and you must tick a box that
says you understand. Add only repositories where a mistake can be undone.

**Merging a pull request is a push too.** `gh pr merge`, `glab mr merge` and `glab mr
accept` follow the same lists. gh and glab have no `-C`, so the command must say which
repository it is:

- `cd ~/code/blog && gh pr merge 12`: the folder in the `cd` is the repository.
- In the repository's own folder, Claude Code removes that `cd` before the guard sees
  it. There, Claude names the repository: `gh pr merge 12 -R owner/name`, or the pull
  request's address.
- A repository named that way must be one of the folder's remotes, or the merge is
  stopped.
- The folder the session is in does not count on its own.

`gh pr merge --admin`, which skips the branch's protection, always asks. Only the command
itself counts: `gh pr merge` written in a pull request's body or a commit message is not
a merge, and neither is an address or `--admin` in the text given to `--body` or
`--subject`.

## Repositories Claude must never touch

Some repositories are not yours alone, or are one wrong push away from production. List
them as **untouchable** and the guard denies `git commit`, `git push` and merging a pull
request there, whatever the other lists say: it wins over `git_allowed_repos` and
`git_ask_repos`. They live in `guard.toml`, one list for the whole computer:

```toml
untouchable_repos = ["~/work/core", "~/work/cli-*"]
```

- Same form as the other lists: `~`, a `*` in the last part, and a worktree counts as its
  repository.
- The answer says the repository is untouchable and that only you can change it. Claude
  is told not to look for another way.
- Add and remove them in the panel's **Guard** page. Removing one asks you to type the
  folder's name, and warns you: from then on the other lists decide, so if the repository
  is in `git_allowed_repos`, Claude will commit and push there.

## Questions that say what they are about

When a repository is in `git_ask_repos`, the question names the repository, the branch
and where the remote leads (the address, never a password): `Branch: feat/x. Remote:
git.example.com/acme/app`. The same for merging a pull request.

## Only you change the guard's lists

The assistant works in the same account as you, so the guard cannot be a wall. It does
three things so that the lists stay yours:

- **It asks before a write to the guard's files** (`config.toml`, `guard.toml`,
  `secrets.toml`, `remote.toml`, `session.toml`, the seal below, and Claude Code's
  settings), or to what runs the guard: the plugin as Claude Code keeps it
  (`~/.claude/plugins/cache/augmented-brain/`, `installed_plugins.json`) and the
  `augmented-brain` program. Copying, unpacking or syncing into the folder that holds
  one of them asks too (`cp -t`, `tar -C`, `rsync`).
- **It denies reaching the panel.** Reading `panel.json` (the panel's key) with a tool
  or a command, and calling a panel page from a command, are denied, however the
  address is written: the panel's Guard page is how you change the lists, and it works
  with that key. `augmented-brain panel` never prints the key either: it prints a link
  that works once, and run by Claude it prints none.
- **It notices a change it did not see.** The guard keeps a seal of its lists: taken
  when you start a session and when you save in the panel. If the lists differ from the
  seal, something else changed them, and a commit, push or merge that the lists would
  let through asks first, and the Guard page and `doctor` say so, until you accept them
  in the Guard page or you start a new session. Meanwhile the lists cannot soften the
  guard: a root exception for this machine does not count, and every `aws` command
  and every `ssh`, `scp` or `rsync` to another machine asks, since a profile or host
  taken out may be what changed. A new session takes the lists as they
  are, and Claude Code tells you so itself. When Claude Code compacts a conversation, or
  after `/clear`, the seal stays: that is not you looking. If the seal cannot be read,
  the guard asks too, and `doctor` says why. The Guard page shows what was added and
  removed since then.
- **It tells you what the panel changed.** A change to the lists made in the panel, or
  lists accepted there, reaches you as a line from Claude Code itself, not from Claude,
  after the next answer or message in your open sessions.

What this does not stop: a script that Claude writes in line (`python -c`, a heredoc) can
still edit the files, as it can anything your account can. The guard then notices the
change and asks before a push, but it did not prevent it. It is a safety net, not a
security boundary.

## Production profiles and untouchable machines

You give them in the first-session interview, or any time: "the AWS profile `shop-prod`
is production", "never touch `db01` without asking me". Claude saves them with the
`safety_save` tool. They hold on the whole machine, in every space.

Claude can only add to these lists. To take one out, use the panel's **Guard** page, or
edit `production_aws_profiles` and `untouchable_hosts` yourself
([Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html)).

These lists are in no backup, because they may name your work's machines. After a
restore on a new machine, the next session offers to ask you for them again.

## Root on one machine, for a while

Sometimes Claude really needs root on a machine, for a migration, say. Add an exception
with an end date to the configuration:

```toml
root_ask = ["db01 until 2026-12-31"]
```

Until that date, root on `db01` asks you each time instead of being stopped. The command
it runs is still checked. After the date, root is stopped again by itself, and
`augmented-brain doctor` says the line can go. The date is required, so no exception is
left behind.

You can also add it in the panel's **Guard** page. It asks you to type the machine's name
again, and reminds you that until that date Claude may run commands as root there, after
you confirm each one. Keep the date close.

## It looks inside

The guard reads what runs inside other commands: `ssh host '…'`, `vagrant ssh -c`,
`docker exec`, `podman exec`, `kubectl exec`, `bash -c`, loops, what a pipe feeds a shell
(`echo 'sudo …' | bash`), short scripts Claude runs (`bash deploy.sh`,
`./deploy.sh`), also when the same command writes them first (`echo '…' > x.sh && bash
x.sh`), `env -S '…'`, and your git aliases (`git ci` when `ci` stands for `commit`). A shell that only checks a script's syntax
(`sh -n install.sh`, `bash -o noexec`) runs nothing, so it is let through. It checks the commands Claude leaves running to watch something, and
those of the helpers Claude starts (subagents and workflows).

## When something is wrong with it

- **The configuration cannot be read.** Then the guard cannot know your lists. It asks
  you before every `aws`, `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync`, `sftp` and `mosh`, and before the tools
  that call AWS. To go back to a version that worked, run `augmented-brain config history`
  and then `augmented-brain config restore <number>`
  ([Configuration versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html)).
- **The program is missing or broken.** Claude Code stops every command and file change
  instead of letting them through (Claude Code 2.1.295 or later; `doctor` warns about an
  older one). If the guard itself fails while checking, it refuses that one action and
  Claude tells you: it is a bug in augmented brain, which you can report from the
  panel's Help page.
- **The configuration folder is unknown** (no `HOME`, as in some services and
  containers), **or `config.toml` is gone but the rest is still there.** The guard asks,
  as when the configuration cannot be read.
- **`guard.toml` cannot be read.** The guard asks before every commit and push until it
  is fixed or removed.
- `augmented-brain doctor` tries the guard for real and tells you if it is not working.

## Next

- [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html): every list, with an example.
- [Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html): when the guard stops something it should not.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/how-it-works.html

# How it works inside


augmented brain is one small program and a folder of notes. This page is how the pieces
fit. To use it, you do not need any of this.

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="../img/how-layers-narrow.en.svg">
  <img alt="augmented brain in four layers" src="../img/how-layers.en.svg">
</picture>

## Four layers

| Layer | What it is | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| **3 · You and your assistant** | You talk to Claude Code as usual. No new commands to learn. | Your terminal or the Claude app |
| **2 · The plugin** | The doors Claude uses to reach the program: a few hooks and an MCP server. | Inside Claude Code, which installs it |
| **1 · The program** | `augmented-brain`, a single file. It guards commands, keeps tasks, rebuilds the index and runs the backup. | `~/.local/bin/augmented-brain` |
| **0 · Your files** | Plain text: the configuration, your notes and, if you want, their backup. | `~/.config/augmented-brain/`, `~/augmented-brain/` and your git repository |

Put another way: **your notes are a notebook, the program keeps it in order and the
plugin is the door.** You only talk to Claude. Claude comes in through the door, and the
program writes in the notebook.

Two words that come up a lot:

- **Hook**: a call Claude Code makes at a given moment. Here: when a session starts,
  before Claude answers each message (to tell it which tasks changed in another session),
  before every command and file change, after each answer, when a long conversation is
  compacted, and when the session ends. Each time, Claude Code starts the program, asks
  it, and the program exits.
- **MCP** (Model Context Protocol): an open standard to give tools to an assistant. The
  program offers its own ("open a task", "park it") and Claude uses them. Since it is a
  standard, other assistants will be able to use the same ones.

The list of hooks is in [Commands](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html#augmented-brain-hook). The tools are in
[MCP tools](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html).

## A session, step by step

<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="../img/how-session-narrow.en.svg">
  <img alt="A session, step by step" src="../img/how-session.en.svg">
</picture>

**1. You open Claude.** The start hook looks at the folder you are in and picks your
[space](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html). Before you type anything, it hands Claude your profile, your rules
and the list of live tasks. It also says what is due soon, whether the weekly review is
due, and whether an earlier session was cut off. That is how Claude knows where you left
off. A session opened for a task (`session start`) hears only that task's dates.

**2. You say "park it".** Claude uses the `task_park` tool. The program writes in the
task file where it stopped and what comes next, and rebuilds the index. Opening,
resuming and closing work the same way. See [Tasks](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/tasks.html).

**3. Claude is about to run a command.** The guard hook reads it first, and lets it
through, asks you, or stops it. See [The guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html).

**4. Claude finishes an answer.** If the session has a task open and nothing was written
in it for 20 minutes, a hook reminds Claude to write in its journal, once. Each session
has its own task, so two windows never get each other's reminder. The same hook looks at the
memory of the window: if it has grown far past normal, Claude tells you, so you can park
the task before the system closes the window. See
[Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html#the-window-uses-a-lot-of-memory).

**5. You close the session.** The end hook notes that the session ended well. It starts
the [backup](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html) of the space in the background, if you set one up. You wait for
nothing. If the network does not answer, the backup gives up after 3 minutes instead of
hanging. If the backup fails, Claude tells you at the start of the next session.

If a session did not end well (the window was closed by force, the computer went down),
the next one offers to recover it. Claude reads what you both said after the task's last
journal entry, from Claude Code's own record of the conversation on this computer (kept
30 days), and writes down what is missing.

## Where files live

Your notes, one folder per space:

```
~/augmented-brain/
├── work/                 a work folder: open Claude here for work
│   ├── notes/
│   │   ├── MEMORY.md     the index Claude reads at the start (written by the program)
│   │   ├── inbox.md      quick notes, to sort out later
│   │   ├── areas/        what you always look after
│   │   ├── tasks/        one file per task
│   │   ├── knowledge/    how things work and what you learned
│   │   ├── people/       who you deal with
│   │   ├── rules/        rules for this space only
│   │   ├── reviews/      weekly reviews
│   │   ├── docs/         long documents of a task; never loaded
│   │   └── archive/      old stuff; never loaded, never deleted
│   └── (your projects)
└── personal/             the same, for personal things
```

The configuration folder, `~/.config/augmented-brain/` (on Windows,
`%APPDATA%\augmented-brain`):

```
config.toml       the spaces and the guard's lists
guard.toml        the repositories Claude must never touch
remote.toml       remote access, if you set it up
session.toml      session settings (the preferred model)
secrets.toml      the names of your secrets, never their values
profile.md        who you are, for every space
shared/           rules, references and lessons for every space
state/            what this computer knows of each space's sessions; never backed up
migrations/       a full copy of the notes before a new version moves them
panel.json        where the panel listens, while it runs
history/          the last 10 versions of these files; only on this computer
```

Each file is described in [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html) and in the
[memory format](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html).

## What it does not do

- **No server and no account.** If Claude is not open, nothing runs, except the panel
  while you use it, the backup that the end of a session starts and, if you set it up,
  [remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html), which keeps running so you can reach your sessions from
  another device.
- **It sends your data to no one.** Only the backup, if you set it up, talks to your
  repository. Apart from that, once a day, it asks GitHub which version is the latest,
  sending nothing of yours. `AB_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` turns that off.
- **It does not change your Claude Code settings.** The plugin goes in and out with
  Claude Code's own commands, which the installer, `update` and `uninstall` run for you.
- **Mind this: your assistant reads your notes**, like any file it opens. They travel
  with your conversations to its provider. Do not keep there what you would not share.

## Moved from this page

This page used to hold more. Each part now has a page of its own:

- <a id="your-files"></a><a id="work-and-personal-apart"></a><a id="shared-notes"></a>Your files, spaces and shared notes: [Spaces](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html) and [Areas, knowledge and the rest](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/notes.html).
- <a id="the-backup"></a><a id="on-a-new-machine"></a>The backup, and a new machine: [Backup and restore](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html).
- <a id="bring-in-a-memory-you-already-have"></a>Importing an existing memory: [Bring in a memory](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/import.html).
- <a id="the-panel"></a>The panel and every page in it: [The panel](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html).
- <a id="update-it"></a><a id="remove-it"></a>Updating and removing it: [Installing](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/install.html#updating).

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/what-claude-may-do.html

# What Claude may do without asking you


Claude works in your account, on your files. Two things decide what it may do on its own:
**Claude Code's permissions** and **augmented brain's guard**. This page puts them side by
side, so you know what happens without a question, what asks you first, and what never
happens.

## Two checks, one after the other

1. **The guard** looks at every command and file change before it runs. It stops some
   things, asks you about others, and lets the rest through. See [The guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html).
2. **Claude Code's permissions** then decide too: the mode you run it in (it asks before
   acting, by default) and the rules you added. Some modes have a check of their own that
   can stop an action the guard would let through.

Both must say yes. A yes from the guard never skips a question from Claude Code, and the
other way round.

## Never, whatever you say

- Becoming root, unless you open an exception for one machine until a date (below).
- Writing a secret in a command or a note: a password, a token, a key.
- Wiping your home folder or the whole disk.
- Anything in a repository you marked as **untouchable**: no commit, push or merge there,
  whatever the other lists say.

Claude tells you what it wanted and gives you the command, for you to run.

## It asks you each time

- **Commit, push or merge in a repository of the "ask" list.**
- **A push that rewrites what is on the remote** (`--force` and the like), even where
  Claude may push. Always, by design.
- **Merging with `--admin`**, which skips the branch's protection.
- **Production:** an `aws` command with a profile you marked as production, and `ssh` to a
  machine you marked as untouchable.
- **Root on a machine with an exception**, each command, until the exception's date.

## Without asking, because you said so

- **Commit and push in a repository of the "allowed" list**, when you asked for that
  change. A merge too, when the command names the repository: `cd ~/code/blog && gh pr
  merge 12`, or, already in that folder, `gh pr merge 12 -R owner/blog`.

Everything else Claude does on its own is reading, writing your notes, and running
ordinary commands: the guard lets them through, and Claude Code's mode decides.

## The lists are yours

The lists live in the configuration, and you change them in the panel's **Guard** page.
Claude cannot open that page, and the guard asks before Claude writes the configuration
files. Some pages warn on purpose: adding a repository where Claude commits and pushes
without asking needs a box ticked, and so on.

## First accept, then use

The guard keeps a **seal** of the lists you last accepted. If the lists change anywhere
else (by hand, a script, another program), what they newly allow does not count yet:

- every commit, push or merge they would let through **asks you first**;
- the Guard page shows **what changed** (what was added and what was removed, list by
  list) and a button to accept it;
- `augmented-brain doctor` says so too.

Accept in the panel, or start a new session, and the new lists apply. A command can be
run by Claude, so `augmented-brain config restore` never accepts lists for you.

## Root on one machine, for a while

For a job that needs it, add an exception with an end date in the Guard page: root on that
machine asks you for each command until the date, and is stopped again after it by
itself. Keep the date close.

## When you want to change something

- To let Claude commit in a repository, add it in the Guard page, to the "ask" list first.
- To have Claude Code ask less, change its own permissions, not the guard: the guard is
  about what must never happen.
- If a command is stopped and you think it should not be, Claude says why. Tell it what
  you wanted; it gives you the command to run yourself.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/where-things-live.html

# Where everything lives, and how it is kept safe


augmented brain keeps everything in plain files on your computer. This page says where each
thing is, what keeps it safe, and what travels in the backup and what never does.

## Your notes

**Where:** one folder per space, inside its work folder: `~/augmented-brain/work/notes/`,
say (`notas` in Spanish). Tasks, areas, knowledge, people, the inbox, the index
`MEMORY.md`. Markdown files you can open and read.

**How they are kept safe:**

- **Only you can read them.** The folder is private to your user; `augmented-brain check`
  closes it again if it was opened.
- **No secrets inside.** Claude's tools refuse to write a password, a token or a key into a
  note.
- **Never half written.** Every change is checked first and written in one go, so a crash
  leaves the note as it was.
- **The backup**, if you set it up: the notes folder is a git repository, copied to a
  private repository of yours at the end of every session. See [Backup and
  restore](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html).

## The configuration

**Where:** one folder per computer, the configuration folder:
`~/.config/augmented-brain/` on Linux and macOS, `%APPDATA%\augmented-brain\` on Windows.

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `config.toml` | The spaces and the guard's lists for the whole computer. |
| `guard.toml` | The repositories nothing may touch. |
| `secrets.toml` | The **names** of your secrets and what each is for. Never a value. |
| `session.toml` | The model your sessions should use. |
| `remote.toml` | Remote access: which spaces have a door. |
| `profile.md` | Who you are and how you like to work. |

**How it is kept safe:**

- **The guard asks** before Claude writes any of these files.
- **Versions.** The last 10 versions are kept, with who made each change: going back
  takes one command, even if `config.toml` was left broken. See [Configuration
  versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html). Only on this computer.
- **The seal.** The guard notices when its lists changed outside the panel, and asks
  before using them. See [What Claude may do without asking you](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/what-claude-may-do.html).

## What this computer knows

Also in the configuration folder, never backed up:

- `state/`: what each space's sessions did (each one's active task, a session that did
  not end well), the guard's seal, the Claude sessions running.
- `history/`: the configuration's versions.
- `panel.json`: where the panel listens while it runs, and its key. Claude is never let
  read it.
- `migrations/`: a full copy of the notes, kept before a new version moved them to its
  format.
- `marketplace/`: the Claude Code plugin, as the program carries it (below).

## Your secrets

The values stay in your system's keychain (or wherever you keep them): augmented brain
never stores them. Only their names are written down, in `secrets.toml`, so you and a new
machine know which secrets there are. The panel's **Secrets** page says which ones this
computer's keychain has.

## What the backup takes, and what it leaves

| Goes in the backup | Never goes |
|---|---|
| Every note of the space | The values of your secrets |
| The space's own settings: its folders and its lists | The lists for the whole computer: production profiles, untouchable machines and repositories, root exceptions |
| In the default space only: your profile, the shared notes and the names of your secrets | The configuration's versions, `state/` and `panel.json` |

The lists for the whole computer stay out because they may name your work's machines.
The repositories where Claude may commit or push travel with the space, but a restore
does not use them, since someone could have changed the backup: it names them, and you add
them again if you still want to.

## The program and the plugin

- The program: `~/.local/bin/augmented-brain` (`augmented-brain.exe` on Windows).
- The Claude Code plugin travels inside the program: it writes it to `marketplace/` in
  the configuration folder, and Claude Code reads it from there. So its hooks are always
  the ones of the version you installed, and the guard asks before Claude changes them.

Uninstalling removes these two and leaves your notes. See [Updating and uninstalling
without losing anything](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/update-and-uninstall.html).


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/phrases.html

# What to say to Claude


You do not learn commands. You talk to Claude in your own words, in English or Spanish,
and it uses augmented brain's tools behind the scenes. These are phrases that work. Any
wording with the same meaning works too.

## Tasks

| You say | What happens |
|---|---|
| "New task: move the blog to a new host." | Opens a task in definition, waiting on you, and asks what "done" means |
| "Where were we?" | Lists your live tasks, those waiting on you first, each with its next step |
| "Let's carry on with the blog." | Reads the task, checks the real state, and picks it up where you left it |
| "Go on to the plan." | Moves the task to its next phase; you approve each change. If you skip a phase, the journal says which |
| "We go with the cheaper host." | Writes the decision in the task's journal, with the date |
| "Add a step: switch the domain." | Adds a checkbox to the task's plan |
| "The database is copied." | Ticks that step |
| "That part waits on Diego: make it a subtask." | Opens a subtask with its own status and next step |
| "On the 16th, check the certificate is renewed." | Adds a watch date to the task |
| "Park it, we carry on tomorrow." | Writes the exact next step and the essentials, and pauses the task |
| "Leave it for some day." | Parks it as someday: out of the daily list, kept in its area |
| "Close the task." | Closes it with its result; it is never deleted. A closed task stays closed: closing it again is refused |
| "Reopen the blog task: the certificate failed again." | Opens it again; the reason goes to its journal |

## Inbox and reminders

| You say | What happens |
|---|---|
| "Note this: look at the new hosting prices." | One dated line in the inbox, no task opened |
| "Remind me on Thursday to call the insurance." | A capture with a date: it comes up at the start of the session |
| "Let's do the weekly review." | Goes through the inbox and the stalled tasks with you, one at a time |

## Knowledge, rules and people

| You say | What happens |
|---|---|
| "Save that as a lesson." | A lesson, with a title that states the conclusion |
| "Write down how the deploy works." | A reference, in the task's area |
| "The newsletter is a new area." | Creates the area |
| "From now on, answer in short sentences." | A rule, loaded in every session |
| "This holds everywhere." | Saves the rule or lesson as shared, for every space |
| "Diego runs the hosting company; I call him Dieguito." | Saves Diego as a person, with his nickname |
| "Why did we pick the cheaper host?" | Finds the decision in your notes, with date and reason |
| "Change my profile: I prefer the recommendation first." | Rewrites your profile |

## Safety

| You say | What happens |
|---|---|
| "The AWS profile shop-prod is production." | The guard asks you before commands that use it |
| "Never touch db01 without asking me." | The guard asks you before ssh, scp or rsync to it |
| "I stored a new secret, telegram/alerts-bot, for alerts to my phone." | Writes down its name and what it is for, never its value |

## Backup, sessions and the panel

| You say | What happens |
|---|---|
| "Set up the backup." | Creates a private repository in your GitHub and makes the first copy |
| "Recover the session that was cut off." | Reads what was said after the last journal entry, and writes down what is missing |
| "~/code/blog is the blog, built with Hugo." | Writes that line for the repository, shown in the panel |
| `/brain:panel` | Opens the panel in your browser |

## When Claude talks first

At the start of a session, Claude may bring things up without being asked:

- a watch date or reminder due in the next 7 days, or already past;
- the weekly review, when the last one is a week old and there is something to go
  through;
- a session that was cut off, to recover;
- a backup that failed, or one that left files out;
- a new version, to update;
- notes with problems;
- what another space sent to this one, until it is done;
- the guard's lists, if something changed them outside the panel.

## Next

- [MCP tools](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html): the tool behind each phrase, and what it takes.
- [The panel](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html): the same things, by clicking.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html

# The panel


The **panel** is a page in your browser to see and change your spaces without going
through Claude. Open it with `/brain:panel` in Claude, or from a terminal:

```bash
augmented-brain panel
```

It opens your browser on **Today**, with the space of the folder you ran it in. If it
cannot (on a computer with no screen, say), it prints an address to open yourself. That
address opens the panel **once**, within 2 minutes; run the command again for another.
When Claude runs it for you, it opens the browser and Claude never sees an address that
opens the panel.

The panel changes your notes the same way Claude does, with the same program, and they
wait for each other: you can have both open at once.

Every page starts with a few words on what it is and what it is for, and a link to its
part of this guide. Once you know your way around, **Hide this help** hides it on that
page, and **Hide it on every page** on all of them. The panel remembers it on this
computer; **What is this page?** brings it back.

## Today

The first page: every space at once. For each one:

- what is due in the next 7 days;
- the tasks waiting on you (the parked ones in one line);
- how many captures wait in the inbox;
- whether the weekly review is due;
- the sessions that were cut off, each with **Keep it in the notes** and **Mark as
  reviewed** (see [Sessions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html#sessions));
- notes with problems.

Below, **Repositories**: those your open tasks name in `repos:` that hold changes not
committed or commits not pushed. That is work that is only on this computer. One whose
tasks are all parked (or left for some day) is marked "forgotten?", here and on the
whole map; a clean one never is. A branch never
pushed counts only if the repository has a remote (a copy on a server,
such as GitHub) to push it to. **See all
repositories** leads to the whole map.

## Tasks

Grouped by area, those waiting on you first, with their status and next step. Filters
show only those waiting on you, under way, parked, untouched, or waiting on one person.
A task nobody has changed for 14 days is marked "untouched N days".

Open one. Its essentials come first, the other sections folded, and the journal newest
first. Write in its journal, change its status or next step, tick its steps, park it or
close it. You can open new tasks too. A closed task opens again only if you choose a new
status for it; its journal says it was reopened from the panel. If a status skips
phases, the journal names them. When a task waits on a person you have a note of,
"waits on" leads to them.

When you save a task, only what you changed on the page is saved. If Claude changed
something else in the meantime, that stays. A step is ticked only if it still says what
the page showed.

## Reminders

The watch dates of your tasks (closed ones too) and the inbox reminders: overdue first,
then the next 30 days. Add one, or mark it done.

## Inbox

Capture an idea, mark one as dealt with, or make it a task.

## Weekly review

The [weekly review](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/weekly-review.html), on a page. Each capture becomes a task, a
reference or a lesson, or is dropped. Each task untouched for two weeks goes on as it
is, or goes to some day (or you open it to close it). What you decide is noted as you go,
and kept in the review's record when you finish.

## Areas, knowledge, rules and people

Knowledge and rules show the space's own and the shared ones, marked "shared". You can
create areas and change an area's title and summary.

People are listed once, with a badge for each space they are in. A new person starts in
the space you are in. A person's page is one form: the name stays (a new name would be a
new person), then a role and other names for each space, then a list of details. Each
detail has a box per space; tick where it should show. Empty a detail's text to remove it.
A detail with no box ticked is not saved, and the page says so next to it. There is always
an empty row at the end to add one, and "Another detail" reloads the page with one more
(save first: it does not keep what you typed). The page also shows the tasks that wait on
them and those that link to them.

## Repositories

Your map of repositories: every git repository in the work folders of each space, up to
three folders down. It skips folders inside another repository, hidden folders,
`node_modules` and `vendor`. They are grouped by space, those with work pending first.

For each one: its branch, where it pushes (as `host/owner/name`, never with a password),
files changed, commits not pushed, the open tasks that name it, and one line of yours on
what it is. Write that line right there. It is kept in the space's notes, in the
reference "Repositories" (`knowledge/ref-repositories.md`), so the backup keeps it.
Claude can write it too.

The panel only reads your repositories. Git runs without taking locks, so it never gets
in your way, and it never asks for a password. It only runs inside the work folders, and
links to folders outside them are not followed.

## Secrets
