The names of the secrets you keep in your system keychain (where your computer keeps
passwords), never their values. Each one as `service/name`, what it is for, and which
tasks name it. So you know which there are, and a new machine knows which to ask you for.

**Check the keychain** says whether each one is on this computer. It asks `secret-tool` on
Linux and `security` on macOS; elsewhere it cannot tell. It asks only when you click,
because a locked keychain asks you for its password. When the keychain lacks one, the
page shows the command that stores it (that command asks you for the value). When the
keychain cannot be asked (on Linux with no desktop session, or a locked keychain on
macOS), the secret shows "cannot tell here", not missing: check it there before storing
it again.

You can add a name, or take one off the list (the secret stays in the keychain). Anything
that looks like a value is refused. The list is the same in every space, and lives in
`secrets.toml` (see [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html#secretstoml)).

## Sessions

Your Claude sessions on this computer, from the last 30 days. It is not in the menu:
open it from **Health**, or from a cut-off session on **Today**.

- Those that did not end (closed by force, or cut off when the computer went down) show
  what was said after the last journal entry. Keep it in the notes (it goes to
  `archive/sessions/` with a line in the task's journal) or mark it as reviewed.
- Those running now, and those that ended, with how much disk their transcripts take
  (the files where Claude Code keeps each conversation). You can delete the transcript of
  an ended session; that session can then no longer be resumed.

## Profile

Who you are and how you like to work: the same profile every space uses.

Under **Your assistant** you can give Claude a name and a personality. Every session
starts with them. They change how it talks, never the rules, the guard or its honesty.
With a name, the emails Claude writes in your name end with that name and, under it, a
line the program adds and you cannot remove, such as "Ana's assistant (AI, Claude)": whoever
reads it knows no person wrote it. The page shows that signature. Leave both fields
empty for no name and no personality.

## Guard

Every list the guard answers to, in one page, to read and change:

- **Untouchable repositories**, where Claude never commits, pushes or merges. Removing one
  warns that the other lists decide again for it (if one lets Claude commit and push
  there, it will), and asks you to type the folder's name.
- **Repositories** each space lets Claude commit in, or ask you about, with a form to add
  or remove. The list where Claude commits and pushes without asking carries a warning,
  and adding to it asks you to tick that you understand.
- **Root exceptions**, with the date each ends (the ones that ended are marked). Adding
  one warns what it allows and asks you to type the machine's name again.
- **Production profiles** and **untouchable machines**.
- **The model of your sessions** (`preferred_model` in `session.toml`): when a session
  answers with another one, Claude tells you. Below it, what Claude Code said about its
  model at the last session start.
- The files Claude cannot change on its own.

Your comments in `config.toml` stay where they are. If the lists are not the ones you last
saw (something changed them outside this page), a notice says so and shows what changed:
what was added and what was removed, list by list, compared with the lists you last
accepted (when those are no longer among the kept versions, it says so). Then an accept
button;
until then (or until you start a new session) a commit, push or merge that the lists allow
asks first. Whatever you change or accept here, Claude Code itself tells you in your
open sessions, after the next answer or message, in a line that starts with
"augmented brain · the guard's lists". If you did not do it, look here. Claude cannot
open this page: it never sees the panel's address, and the guard denies it the panel's
key. See [The guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html).

## Versions

The last 10 versions of your configuration (spaces, guard, remote access,
session settings, profile and your secrets' names),
kept only on this computer, newest first, with when and who changed it. **What it
changed** shows the lines of each one; **Go back to this one** makes it the
configuration again, keeping the one you had as a version first. It asks you to tick a
box, and warns first when the guard's lists would change, with what. They are never in
the backup: your notes are, with their own history. From another device
the page only shows. See [Configuration versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html).

## Backup

Whether the notes of each space have a copy elsewhere, in a private repository, so they
survive if this computer breaks. A space with no backup says so in red.

- For a space with a backup: how the last copy went, where it goes, the last copies
  with the date and the computer that made them, and **Back up now**. The copy runs in
  the background and takes a few seconds; reload the page to see how it went. It also
  runs by itself every time a session ends.
- Each copy shows **What it changed**, note by note, with the lines. **Go back to this
  copy** shows first what would change in your notes now, and asks for a box and the
  space's name. What you had is kept as a copy first, so it can be undone. See [Go back
  to a copy](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html#go-back-to-a-copy).
- For a space with none: **Set it up on my GitHub** makes a private repository called
  `augmented-brain-<space>` in your GitHub account and the first copy. It needs the
  GitHub command line, `gh`, installed and logged in; the page says how if it is not.
  **I already have a private repository** takes its address instead.
- **Bring the notes back on another computer** shows the command to run there. Restoring
  is never done from the panel: it is for a computer that does not have the notes yet.

Moving a backup that exists somewhere else is done in a terminal, with `augmented-brain
backup setup`. From another device the page only shows. See [Backup](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html).

## Health

The space's notes folder and work folders, whether it is the default space, notes that
are not valid, repositories that notes point at and that are no longer on this computer,
the index, the last backup, the last weekly review, and a link to the space's
[Sessions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html#sessions).

## Help

Links to the answers on this website, in your language. And a way to tell us about a
problem or propose an idea on GitHub (the website where the project lives; you need a
free account there).

Click **Report a problem on GitHub**. The panel runs the health check (what
`augmented-brain doctor` says) at that moment. Then it opens GitHub's form in a new tab,
with the version, your system and that check filled in.

Before it opens, the panel takes out what is personal: your home folder (shown as `~`),
your notes and work folders, e-mail addresses, the names of your spaces, untouchable
machines, production AWS profiles, and any line that looks like a password or a key.
You write what happened, and read the rest: change or delete what you prefer not to
share. Nothing is sent until you press GitHub's submit button. To be honest about it:
the text travels to GitHub inside the page's address as soon as it opens, so GitHub can
see it then, even if you never submit.

## Search and reading notes

The **search** box at the side looks through the notes of the space and the shared ones:
titles, summaries and text. A note shows up when it holds every word, in any case, with
accents or without.

Notes read as text, not as raw Markdown (the plain-text format notes are
written in): headings, lists, tables, code and links. A
`[[link]]` to another note takes you to it. If a note changes on disk while its page is
open (Claude wrote in it, say), the page tells you, with a link to see it as it is now.

## Made to stay yours

- It runs **only while you use it**. After 30 minutes without use it stops by itself. To
  stop it now: `augmented-brain panel stop`, or the link at the bottom of the page.
- It works **only on this computer**. Other machines on your network cannot reach it.
  To open it from your phone or another computer of yours, use
  `augmented-brain panel remote`: see [The panel from another device](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel-remote.html).
- The address you get opens it **once**. The panel then takes your browser to its
  pages, whose address carries a **key**, made new each time the panel starts. Without
  it the panel answers nothing, so another program or web page on your computer cannot
  use it. Treat the address of the pages like a password: do not share it. It stops
  working when the panel stops. If something else used your link first, your browser
  says "This link was already used" instead of opening: you know.
- It loads **nothing from the internet**: no fonts, no statistics. It works offline. A
  note cannot put HTML or scripts of its own in the page. The links of the Help page go to
  the website only when you click them.
- Checking whether a note changed does not count as using the panel: a tab left open
  does not keep it running.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel-remote.html

# The panel from another device


The [panel](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html) opens on the computer where augmented brain runs, and only there.
To open it from another of your devices, your phone or another computer, augmented
brain uses **[Tailscale](https://tailscale.com)**: a free app that joins your devices in
a private network of their own. Only your devices are in it; nothing is open to the
internet.

```bash
augmented-brain panel remote
```

It starts the panel, publishes it in your Tailscale network, and prints its address,
such as `https://my-laptop.example.ts.net:8443/t/…`, and a QR code. Point the
phone's camera at the code, or open the address on the other computer. The address
opens the panel once, within 10 minutes: run the command again for another.

If the panel is already open on this computer, it is not stopped: the same panel starts
answering through the network too, and the pages you have open go on working. If that
panel came from an earlier version, it has to start again: the command says so, and you
reload those pages. If publishing fails, the panel stays on this computer only.

## What you need, once

The command checks each of these and, when one is missing, says exactly what to do. It
never installs or changes anything of Tailscale's for you.

1. **Tailscale on both devices**, signed in with the same account:
   [tailscale.com/download](https://tailscale.com/download). It works on Linux, macOS,
   Windows, Android and iPhone.
2. **HTTPS in your Tailscale network**, so the panel travels encrypted with a real
   certificate. Turn it on in Tailscale's admin page,
   [login.tailscale.com/admin/dns](https://login.tailscale.com/admin/dns): **HTTPS
   Certificates → Enable HTTPS**. One thing to know: the names of your machines (such
   as `my-laptop.example.ts.net`) then appear in public logs of certificates. Anyone can
   see that the name exists; nobody outside your devices can reach it.
3. **On Linux, let your user publish.** Tailscale lets only an administrator publish on
   the computer. Once, with your administrator password:

   ```bash
   sudo tailscale set --operator=your-user-name
   ```

   augmented brain prints this line with your name and does not run it. On macOS and
   Windows it is not needed.

## Who can open it

Four things keep it yours:

- **Only your Tailscale network reaches the address.** It does not exist on the
  internet.
- **Only your account gets in.** Tailscale tells the panel who sends each request (the
  account you signed in with, with its own password and second factor), and the panel
  lets in only the owner of the computer. Someone else in your network, or someone you
  share a device with, gets "forbidden" even with the address.
- **The network has a door of its own.** What Tailscale brings in arrives at a port of
  the panel that only it uses, and is treated as coming from the network whatever it
  says about itself: from there, nothing that is only for this computer (setting up a
  backup, going back to an earlier configuration) can be done.
- **The address works once**, and the pages it opens hold a key that changes every
  time the panel starts.

There is no extra password to type: your Tailscale account is the login.

## It is always temporary

The address works while the panel runs. The panel stops by itself after 30 minutes
without use, or now with:

```bash
augmented-brain panel stop
```

When it stops, it takes the address back from Tailscale. If the computer crashed or
restarted with the panel published, the next time a panel starts it takes it back, and
`augmented-brain doctor` warns while it is still there. Port 8443 of your Tailscale
network is the panel's: if you already publish something else there (even another
program of this computer), augmented brain leaves it alone and says so. It only ever
takes back the address it published itself.

## Check it

`augmented-brain doctor` has a line about the remote panel once you have used it:
whether Tailscale is still installed, connected and with HTTPS, and whether an address
of the panel was left published.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html

# Configuration versions


Your configuration is what augmented brain knows about this computer and about you:
your spaces, the guard's lists, remote access, your profile and the names of your
secrets. A wrong change there (a list emptied by mistake, a space pointing to the wrong
folder) used to have no way back. Now every change is kept as a **version**, and you can
see what changed and go back.

## What is kept

A version is a copy of these files, in the configuration folder, as they were at one
moment: `config.toml`, `guard.toml`, `remote.toml`, `session.toml`, `profile.md` and
`secrets.toml` (only the names of your secrets, never a value). It also says who made the
change: the panel, a command, the assistant (and with which tool), going back to an
earlier version, or by hand.

- A new version is kept every time the configuration changes. A change made by hand, or
  by an older program, is kept the next time augmented brain looks: when a session
  starts, a command runs, the assistant uses a tool or you save something in the panel.
- The last **10** are kept. When there is one more, the oldest goes.
- They stay **only on this computer**, in the `history` folder of the configuration
  folder. They never go into the backup: the guard's lists may name work machines, and
  the backup leaves them out on purpose.
- Your notes are not here. Tasks, rules, knowledge and people (shared ones too) have
  their own history in the [backup](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html).

## In the panel

The panel's **Versions** page lists them, newest first, with when and who. Under each
one, **What it changed** shows the lines that changed from the version before: green
what was added, red what was taken away. **Go back to this one** makes it the
configuration again: it opens first, says what going back does and, when the guard's
lists would change, which entries each list would gain or lose. Tick the box to confirm,
then go back.

Going back keeps the configuration you had as a version first, so it can be undone the
same way. A version that would leave a file the program cannot read is refused, and
nothing changes. If the guard's lists change, going back from the panel counts as you
accepting them, as any change on the [Guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html) page does.

From another device ([the panel from another device](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel-remote.html)) the page only
shows the versions: going back is only from the panel on this computer, because it can
change what the guard allows.

## With commands

```bash
augmented-brain config history
augmented-brain config history 3
augmented-brain config restore 3
```

`config history` lists the versions; with a number, it shows what that one changed.
`config restore` goes back to one. A command can be run by the assistant, so going back
this way never accepts new guard lists for you: until you accept them in the panel's
Guard page, or start a new session, the guard asks before every commit, push or merge it
used to allow. See [Commands](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html#augmented-brain-config-history).

Both work even when `config.toml` is broken and nothing else will start: that is when
going back helps most. `augmented-brain doctor` then says so, and points to them.

`augmented-brain doctor` has a line with how many versions are kept, and says when the
configuration changed after the newest one.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/weekly-review.html

# The weekly review


On Monday you open Claude. It says: "The weekly review is due: 3 captures in the inbox
and 1 task untouched for two weeks. Shall we do it? About ten minutes." You say yes, and
it goes through each item with you, one at a time.

The **weekly review** keeps the system honest. Without it, the inbox fills up and stalled
tasks pile up in silence.

## What it goes through

- **The inbox,** with what other spaces sent here, marked with where it came from. Each
  capture becomes a task, goes to an area or to knowledge, or is
  dropped.
- **Tasks untouched for 14 days or more.** Each one goes on as it is, goes to someday, or
  is closed.
- **The dates due in the coming week**: watch dates of tasks and inbox reminders.

## When it comes up

At the start of a session, when the last review is 7 days old or more (with no review yet,
since the oldest capture or untouched task) and there is something to go through. Claude offers it once, in one line, when it does not interrupt
other work. You can also ask for it any time: "let's do the weekly review".

## With Claude

Claude lists what there is, then asks about each item. You decide; it does the rest:
opens the task, files the note, drops the capture. At the end it saves what was decided
and takes the processed captures out of the inbox.

## In the panel

The panel has a **Weekly review** page. Each capture has its buttons: a task, a
reference, a lesson, or drop it. Each untouched task goes on, or goes to some day (or you
open it to close it). What you decide is noted as you go, in a draft on this computer,
so you can leave and come back. When you finish, it is all written in the review's
record.

## What is kept

Each review is a note, `reviews/review-<date>.md`, with what was decided. Processed
captures leave the inbox. Nothing else is deleted.

## Two computers

Captures added on two computers are both kept. One catch: a capture you processed on one
computer can come back if the other computer captured something at the same time. It
just shows up again at the next review.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html

# Backup and restore


Your laptop dies. On the new one, you install augmented brain, run one command, and open
Claude. It carries on where you left off: tasks, notes, rules and your profile.

That is the **backup**. The notes folder of each space is also a git repository (git keeps
every version of a folder and can copy it to a server). The backup pushes it to a private repository of yours, one per space.

## Set it up: ask Claude

Say "set up the backup". Claude offers it at the end of the first-session interview too.

It creates a private repository in your GitHub account, `augmented-brain-<space>`,
connects it and makes the first copy. For that it uses `gh`, GitHub's official command
line. If you do not have it, Claude tells you how to install it, and walks you through
the one step that needs your browser: logging in.

Rather somewhere else (GitLab, your company's git)? Do it yourself, in a folder of the
space:

```bash
augmented-brain backup setup git@gitlab.com:lucia/brain-work.git
```

Claude does not take an address for this: one it was handed by a page or a message it
read would send all your notes there. Use a **private** repository: your notes are in
it. And an address without a password: it is kept in the configuration and inside the
backup itself, so `backup setup` refuses one. Let git keep the login instead (for
GitHub, `gh auth setup-git`; or an ssh address like the one above). If an earlier version
kept one, `augmented-brain doctor` tells you how to take it out.

The panel's [Backup](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html#backup) page does the same with two buttons, and shows
each space's last copies and a **Back up now**.

Until a space has a backup, augmented brain says so: `augmented-brain doctor` names each
space with none, `update` warns when it goes ahead with no copy to go back to, and
`uninstall --all` warns that those notes will be gone for good.

## It runs by itself

From then on, **the backup runs every time a Claude session ends**, in the background.
You wait for nothing. A space that this session wrote in from another space (a task of
another space) is backed up then too. If it fails (no network, no access to the repository), Claude tells
you at the start of the next session.

You can also run it by hand:

```bash
augmented-brain backup          # this folder's space
augmented-brain backup --all    # every space
```

To turn the automatic backup off, set `AB_NO_AUTO_BACKUP=1` in your environment.

## On a new machine

1. Install augmented brain with the usual command. It creates the spaces, empty. If
   Claude opens at the end, close it without doing the interview: your profile comes in
   the backup.
2. If the repository is on GitHub, log in once with `gh auth login`, so git has access.
3. Bring each space back from its backup:
   ```bash
   augmented-brain restore https://github.com/lucia/augmented-brain-work.git
   ```
   It replaces the empty space with yours: notes, tasks, rules and the space's settings,
   readable by you only. If anything fails half way, the empty space stays as it was. If
   that space already had notes of yours, it leaves it alone.

   The notes go where they were on the old machine, as long as that is inside your home
   folder. A backup cannot choose a place outside it, or in its hidden or system folders
   (`~/.config`, `~/Library`, `~/AppData`, any `.git`): your computer runs some of what
   it finds there, and someone else may have changed the backup. Then the space goes to
   `~/augmented-brain/<space>`, and `restore` tells you. To choose the place yourself,
   use `--memory` and `--work`.
4. Open Claude. It carries on where you left off, and the backup keeps running by itself.

Restore the default space (`personal`) too: your profile, your shared notes and the list
of your secrets' names come with it.

## Go back to a copy

A note got broken, or deleted by mistake? Open the panel's **Backup** page. Each copy
shows **What it changed**: the notes it added, changed and removed, with their lines.

To have your notes as they were in one copy, use **Go back to this copy**:

1. A page shows what would change in your notes as they are now, note by note. Notes
   that no copy holds yet show up too, as removed.
2. Tick the box and type the space's name.
3. What you have now is kept first, as a new copy. Then your notes become those of the
   copy you picked, and that is kept as a copy too. The next backup sends it.

To undo it, go back to the copy made just before. Going back touches the notes of that
space only, never your configuration (that is [Versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html)). It is done
from this computer's panel only: from another device the page only shows.

## What a restore does not bring

Some things are left out on purpose:

- **The guard's lists**: production AWS profiles and untouchable machines. They may name
  your work's machines, so they are in no backup. `restore` and `doctor` say so, and the
  next session offers to ask you for them again. Until then, nothing asks before touching
  production.
- **The repositories where Claude may commit and push** (`git_allowed_repos` and
  `git_ask_repos`). Someone else may have changed the backup, so `restore` names them,
  and you add them again if you still want to.
- **Your secrets' values.** Only their names travel. `restore` names the secrets this
  machine's keychain does not have yet, each with the command to store it, and those it
  could not check when the keychain does not answer, or on Windows, where it cannot be
  asked.

## What you get

- **Several machines, one brain.** Before pushing, the backup fetches what your other
  machine did and merges it. A task where each machine only wrote in the journal, or
  where one moved old entries to `archive/journals/` while the other wrote, joins by
  itself.
- **Full history.** Every backup is a git commit, with the machine and the time. The
  panel shows what each one changed and goes back to it; with `git log` you see all of
  them.
- **Your place.** GitHub, GitLab or your own server: you pick the repository. augmented
  brain has no cloud.
- **One repository per space.** Work can go to your company's git, and personal to
  yours. Your profile only travels in the default space's backup, never in the work one.
- **No secrets go up.** Claude's tools refuse to write a password or a token into a note.
  If one gets in anyway (by hand, say), the backup stops and tells you which file.
- **Nothing gets overwritten.** If two machines changed the same note, the backup stops
  without touching anything and explains how to sort it out. When each machine only added
  journal entries to it, they are joined by themselves, in date order. The index is
  rebuilt by itself, and captures in the inbox from two machines are both kept.
- **No junk, no giants.** Leftovers of a crash and the files systems drop in folders
  (`.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`) stay out. A file over 50 MB stays out too (GitHub refuses
  them), and Claude tells you which one.

## When it fails

Claude tells you at the start of the next session, with the reason. Running
`augmented-brain backup` in a folder of the space shows the problem. The usual ones are
in [Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html#the-backup-failed).

It also tells you when a backup began and never ended (the computer went off half way),
and when the last good one is over 3 days old and your notes changed since: the
automatic backup is not running (say, `AB_NO_AUTO_BACKUP` was left set). `doctor` says
the same.

Your git settings for your code do not get in the way: the backup never signs its
commits, never runs your global hooks (`core.hooksPath`) and never opens a window asking
for a password. A credential helper that already has it (`gh`'s, your keychain's) still
works.

Backups go to the branch `main`, and `restore` reads them from there, even from a
repository whose default branch is another (one made with `git init --bare` on a
server, say).

A backup never hangs: each step stops after 3 minutes without an answer (or a download
slower than 1 KB a second for a minute), and a backup waits at most 10 minutes for
another one to finish. Both say why.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/connect-services.html

# Connect your services


augmented brain keeps your tasks and notes. To read your calendar, your mail, your
documents or your tickets, your assistant also needs those services. Claude Code talks to
them through **MCP** (Model Context Protocol): small connectors that give it tools such as
"list today's meetings" or "read this Jira issue".

## The easy way: claude.ai connectors

If you sign in to Claude Code with your claude.ai account, the connectors you turn on in
claude.ai also work in Claude Code.

1. Open **claude.ai → Settings → Connectors**.
2. Connect the services you want: Google Calendar, Gmail, Google Drive, Atlassian (Jira
   and Confluence), and others. Each one asks you to sign in to that service once.
3. **Start a new Claude Code session.** Connectors load when a session starts: a session
   that was already open will not see a connector you just added.
4. In Claude Code, type `/mcp` to see them. A connector marked as needing authentication
   is fixed from claude.ai, not from Claude Code.

That is all. Your assistant uses them when a task needs them ("what meetings do I have
tomorrow?", "summarise the open issues of this epic").

## Without a claude.ai account

If you use Claude Code with an API key (a code from the Anthropic Console instead of
your claude.ai account), claude.ai connectors are not available. You can
add MCP servers yourself:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user <name> -- <command that starts the server>
```

Many services publish an official MCP server; use those when they exist. Read what a
server can do before adding it: it acts with your account.

## Good habits

- **Connect only what you use.** Every connector adds tools your assistant has to choose
  from.
- **Your safety rules still apply.** augmented brain's guard watches commands and file
  writes. Actions inside a connector (sending an email, editing a ticket) are confirmed
  through Claude Code's own permission prompts: read them before you accept.
- **Never paste a password or a token in the chat** to connect a service. Every connector
  signs in through the service's own page.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html

# Remote access


Claude Code can be reached from another computer or from your phone: from
[claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) or Claude Desktop you pick a session that runs on
your machine and work in it as if you were sitting there. For that, a small program,
`claude remote-control`, has to be running on the machine.

`augmented-brain remote` keeps it running for you. It starts by itself, and starts again
if it stops. You set it up once. It works on the three systems, each with its own way of
starting programs by themselves:

- **Linux**: a user service of systemd (the part of Linux that starts and watches
  services). It can start when the computer starts, before anyone logs in. Not in a
  container, nor in WSL without systemd.
- **macOS**: a LaunchAgent, the way macOS starts a program when you log in.
- **Windows**: a task of the Task Scheduler that starts when you log in, with no window.

On macOS and Windows it starts **when you log in**, not before: after a reboot, log in
once and it is back. Neither system lets an ordinary user start something with nobody
logged in, and augmented brain never asks for an administrator.

## One door per space

Each space (work, personal…) gets its own door, with its own name:
`<computer name>-<space>`, such as `my-laptop-personal`. A session opened through that door
starts in a folder that belongs to that space, so Claude loads that space's notes and
rules, and nothing crosses between spaces. By default only your default space has a door.
To open one for work too, see [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html).

That folder is the space's first work folder, the one you named when you made the space:
where you already work, so a session from your phone opens where you would open one at
the computer. To start somewhere else inside the space, set `folders` in
[`remote.toml`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html). Only a space with no work folder gets a folder of its
own, `~/.config/augmented-brain/remote/<space>`.

## Install it

```bash
augmented-brain remote install
```

It checks that the system can keep the service, writes it and starts it. If it cannot,
it says why and changes nothing. It then tells you what is missing, if anything:
one thing only you can do, two on Linux.

### 1. Let Claude trust the folder

Claude refuses to run in a folder it has not been told to trust, and there is no one at
the keyboard to answer when it starts by itself. If you already use Claude in your work
folder, it trusts it and there is nothing to do. Otherwise, once for each folder `install`
names, open Claude there and accept the question:

```bash
cd ~/projects && claude
```

On Windows, in PowerShell, `install` writes it as `cd "C:\Users\you\projects"; claude`.
Accept "trust this folder", then close Claude (`/exit`). augmented brain never edits
Claude's own settings for you. The service tries again by itself (every 30 seconds, every
minute on Windows), so within a minute it is running.

### 2. On Linux, turn on "linger"

A user service normally runs only while you are logged in. To have it after a reboot with
nobody logged in, the system must be told to keep your services: that is called
**linger**, and it needs an administrator. `install` prints the exact command and does
not run it:

```bash
sudo loginctl enable-linger your-user-name
```

macOS and Windows have no linger: there the service starts when you log in.

## Check it

```bash
augmented-brain remote status
```

For each space it says whether the service is running, whether Claude trusts its folder,
and on Linux whether linger is on, with what to do about each problem. On Linux it also
says how the watch stands (the one that brings back a service whose server archived the
session, see below): whether it is running and how long ago it last looked.
`augmented-brain doctor` shows the same, one line per space, and one more for the watch
only when it fails.

When a service fails, it says why. On Linux, in the system journal:

```bash
journalctl --user -u augmented-brain-remote-personal -n 20
```

On macOS, in `~/Library/Logs/augmented-brain/augmented-brain-remote-<space>.log`; on
Windows, in `augmented-brain-remote-<space>.log` inside
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\augmented-brain\remote`. `status` names the file.

A service installed by an earlier version sent its errors nowhere; `status` and `doctor`
tell you to run `augmented-brain remote install` again, which brings it up to date.

## Connect from another computer

1. Open [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) or Claude Desktop, signed in to the same
   Claude account as on the machine.
2. Choose the environment named `<computer name>-<space>`, the name `status` shows.
3. Start a session. Start as many as you like: each one begins in that space's folder.

## A session per task

This part is for Linux only for now: it has been tried only there. On macOS and Windows
`session start` says it is not available.

The door's own sessions all start in the space's folder. To work on a task in its own
session, in its own folder, ask the session you are in: "open me a session for the website
task". Every session on Linux knows how, here or from another computer, because the start
of each one tells it. It runs

```bash
augmented-brain session start task-new-website
```

and within a minute a new session, named after the task, shows up in claude.ai and Claude
Desktop. It starts on its own: it reads its task, tells you where it stands and gets on
with the next step. It hears only what is its task's: that task's dates, not the rest of
the space's reminders, the weekly review or sessions to recover, which come up in your
other sessions. When it stops, it tells the session that asked for it, in one line. The folder is the
first of the task's repositories found in the space's work folders, or the one `--folder`
gives; with no repository, the space's folder. For a bare repository, the task gets a git worktree of its own, on a new branch
from origin's default branch. It goes away by itself when nothing would be lost: with
`session stop`, when the task is closed, or, for a session that ended some other way (a
reboot, closing it from Claude Desktop), at the next `session start`. One with work not
committed or not pushed, or files git ignores such as a `.env`, stays, and `doctor` names
it.

- **Claude must trust that folder itself.** Trusting the space's folder is not enough. The
  first time, the command says what to do: on the machine (or through `ssh`), go to the
  folder, run `claude`, accept the question and close it with `/exit`. Then ask again.
  For a git worktree, Claude keeps the answer under its main repository: trusting either
  one is enough.
- **One task per folder.** Two tasks in one folder would step on each other's changes,
  so a folder another task's session uses is refused. Give it another one with
  `--folder` (a git worktree of the repository, for example).
- **It ends with `augmented-brain session stop <task>`**, which also takes it out of
  Claude Desktop and claude.ai, when its task is closed (once it has finished its
  answer), or when the machine restarts. After a reboot only the
  doors come back: ask for the task sessions again. `augmented-brain session list`
  shows the open ones.
- **Claude retires a session left unused for hours.** It stops running, and claude.ai
  shows it as disconnected. `session list` calls it retired; `session start` with its
  task brings it back with its whole conversation, and `session stop` and closing the
  task close it all the same.
- **It waits on a pull request with `augmented-brain watch pr`.** The session leaves
  [`watch pr`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html#augmented-brain-watch-pr) running in the background with its
  task. When the checks pass or fail, or the pull request is merged, it writes the result
  in the task, so your other sessions hear of it even if this one is gone, and tells
  the session to let you know at once. It never waits for ever: 3 hours at most.
- **A session that cannot work is not left open.** `session start` checks first that
  Claude Code is logged in, then waits for the first answer (up to a minute). If that
  answer is an error, such as an expired login, it closes the session and says what to
  do. A session whose answer fails later shows as failed in `session list`.

## Keep it safe

**This is a permanent door to your computer.** Anyone who gets into your Claude account
can work on the machine through it.

- Claude asks before it acts, as always (permission mode `default`), and the guard stays
  in force: it stops pushes, root and secrets, and asks before production.
- **Do not set `permission_mode` to `bypassPermissions`.** It lets whoever connects run
  anything with no question, and leaves the machine open.
- Protect your Claude account: a strong password and two-step verification.
- Remove the door whenever you do not need it: `augmented-brain remote uninstall`.

## Good to know

- **A laptop that sleeps drops the connection.** The session is back when it wakes up. The
  program does not change your sleep settings.
- **On macOS and Windows, a reboot leaves it off until you log in.** If the computer
  restarts by itself (an update, a power cut), nobody can connect until someone logs in.
- If your Claude login expires, the service keeps running but nobody can connect. `status`
  and `doctor` say so; run `claude` once and sign in again.
- **If the server archives the session** (you archived it in claude.ai, say), on Linux the
  service comes back by itself with a new, empty session of the same name, in about ten
  minutes: a watch looks every two minutes (see
  [`remote watch`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html#augmented-brain-remote-watch)). On macOS and Windows,
  run `augmented-brain remote install` again.
- Sessions you start from the phone belong to the space of their folder: the work door
  opens work notes. To reach another space, use that space's door.

## Take it away

```bash
augmented-brain remote uninstall
```

It stops and removes the services and, on Linux, the watch (on Windows, also the program they were running). The
folders, and their place in the space's work
folders, stay, and nothing else is deleted. Remove them by hand if you want.

## The settings

`remote.toml`, in the configuration folder: `enabled`, `spaces`, `name_prefix`,
`permission_mode` and `folders`. See [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html). The commands are in
[Commands](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html).


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/import.html

# Bring in a memory you already have


If Claude Code has been keeping a memory for you, you do not start from zero. Claude Code
writes it in `~/.claude/projects/<folder>/memory/`. You can bring it into your spaces.

## First, look

```bash
augmented-brain import ~/.claude/projects/<folder>/memory
```

With one space, that is all. With more (a usual install has two), it first asks which
space each note goes to: see [More than one space](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/import.html#more-than-one-space) and add `--map`.

That writes nothing. It shows where each note would go, and what it could not decide:

- files that are not notes (an index, say);
- notes about you: copy what matters into your profile;
- links that would cross from one space to another;
- ids (the name of each note's file, such as `task-blog`) your space already has.

The folder you import from is only read, now and later.

## Then, write

When the list looks right, run it again with `--apply`:

```bash
augmented-brain import ~/.claude/projects/<folder>/memory --apply
```

It never writes over a note that already exists.

## What each file becomes

Each file becomes a note of its kind: by its name (`task-…`, `area-…`, `ref-…`,
`lesson-…`, `rule-…`, `person-…`), or else by what Claude Code says it is. A task with no
status comes in parked, waiting on you, with "review this imported task" as its next
step.

The rest comes along too:

- The captures of your old `inbox.md` (each `- …` line) go to the inbox of the space of
  `*` (below), or the default space, dated, and never twice.
- `archive/` and `docs/<task>/` are copied as they are, next to their note, also when you
  import again later.
- A file with a secret written in it (a key, a token) is imported, but named in the
  report. The backup will not upload it until the secret is out. `augmented-brain check`
  names it too.
- A reference or lesson that is a list of people (one `## Name` section each, with a word
  like "people" or "team" in its id or title) comes in as it is, and the report names it.
  People are notes of their own, so ask Claude to save each one as a person.

## More than one space

A small file says which space each area goes to, which notes go somewhere other than
their area, and which go to the shared notes:

```text
area-family = personal
task-evening-course = work
lesson-git-small-commits = shared
* = work
```

`*` is for everything else; with one space, no file is needed. Pass the file with `--map`:

```bash
augmented-brain import ~/.claude/projects/<folder>/memory --map map.txt
```

If the notes name repositories in `repos:` (the list of folders a task
works in), `--repos-base <folder>` says what those paths
are relative to. They are then rewritten relative to the space's work folder.

## Turn off the old memory

Has Claude Code been keeping that memory by itself? Then it goes on keeping it for your
spaces' folders: a second memory, next to the space's, that drifts from it.
`augmented-brain doctor` tells you, and how to turn it off: `"autoMemoryEnabled": false`
in Claude Code's settings. What it already has stays, ready to import.

All the options: [Commands](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html#augmented-brain-import).


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/anywhere.html

# Working from your phone or another computer


Your notes live on one computer. You can still work with them from your phone, a tablet
or another computer. There are two ways, and they do different things:

- **Talk to Claude** on that computer, from anywhere: [remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html). You pick a
  session in [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) or Claude Desktop, and work as if you
  were sitting there.
- **Look at your notes** in the panel, from anywhere: [the panel from another
  device](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel-remote.html). Today, your tasks, the inbox, everything the panel shows.

You can use one, the other, or both. Remote access works on Linux, macOS and Windows; the
panel from another device works wherever [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) does.

## Set it up once

On the computer that holds your notes:

1. **Remote access.** Run `augmented-brain remote install`, then do what it asks: let
   Claude trust the folder and, on Linux, turn on "linger" so it survives a reboot (on
   macOS and Windows it starts when you log in). Details in [Remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html).
2. **The panel.** Install Tailscale on the computer and on your phone, signed in to the
   same account, then run `augmented-brain panel remote`. It prints an address and a QR
   code. Details in [The panel from another device](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel-remote.html).

`augmented-brain doctor` checks both, one line each.

## Which session to use

Remote access opens **one door per space**, named `<computer name>-<space>`, such as
`my-laptop-personal`. A session started through it begins in that space's first work
folder, so Claude loads that space's notes and rules.

- In claude.ai or Claude Desktop, pick the environment with that name and start a session.
  You can start as many as you like.
- To work on a task, say so: "resume task-bake-bread". Claude reads the task and carries
  on where it was left.
- To reach another space, use that space's door. Notes never cross between spaces.

## When it stops answering

- **The computer is asleep.** A laptop that sleeps drops the connection. It comes back when
  it wakes up.
- **The session was archived.** Archiving a session in claude.ai, or leaving it unused
  for long, can end it on Claude's side while the service on your computer keeps running
  with nothing behind it. Start the service again, on the computer:

  ```bash
  systemctl --user restart augmented-brain-remote-personal
  ```

  The new session can take up to a few minutes to appear: Claude's side first lets the
  old one expire. The watch does this by itself within a few minutes; if you restart
  by hand, run `augmented-brain remote watch` first, so the sessions of your tasks
  started from there keep running.
- **Your Claude login expired.** `augmented-brain remote status` says so. Run `claude`
  once on the computer and sign in again.

`augmented-brain remote status` says how each door stands, and what to do.

## An old session with the same name

When the door of a space moves to another folder (a new version starts it in your work
folder, say), Claude's side keeps the old session too, with the same name, in another
group of the list. Nothing answers in the old one: what you write there is lost. Use the
one in the group named after the new folder, and archive the old one in claude.ai or
Claude Desktop.

## Starting new sessions from the phone

Ask the session behind the space's door to open one for a task ("open me a session for
the website task"). It runs `augmented-brain session start`, and a session of its own for
that task shows up in your list within a minute, named after the task, in its folder,
already reading it. Open as many as you have tasks. The first time in a folder it tells
you how to make Claude trust it. See [A session per task](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html#a-session-per-task).

## Keep it safe

Both are doors to your computer. Remote access is a permanent one: anyone who gets into
your Claude account can work on the machine through it. Protect that account with a strong
password and two-step verification, keep Claude asking before it acts (never
`bypassPermissions`), and remove the doors you do not use: `augmented-brain remote
uninstall` and `augmented-brain panel stop`. The panel's address works only for your own
devices in your Tailscale network, and only while the panel runs.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/update-and-uninstall.html

# Updating and uninstalling without losing anything


Your notes are plain files that belong to you. Updating never touches what they say, and
uninstalling leaves them where they are unless you ask for the opposite. This page says
what each step does, so you can do it calmly.

## Updating

When a new version is out, Claude tells you at the start of a session. To update:

```bash
augmented-brain update
```

What it does, in order:

1. **Checks the installation** and shows what it finds, so a problem that was already
   there is not taken for one of the new version.
2. **Backs up every space that has a backup.** If one fails, it stops and updates nothing:
   that copy is your way back. With no backup at all, it says it goes ahead without one.
3. **Downloads and installs** the new version, with the Claude Code plugin that comes
   inside it. If GitHub fails to hand out the files, it tries three times, also through
   GitHub's API; if all fails, it says so and nothing changes.
4. **Checks the new version is in place**, and restarts the idle Claude sessions that
   still run the old one, one at a time, with the same conversation: a task's session,
   those of the remote access, and those of Claude Desktop, which stay open while only
   their augmented brain restarts. A session that is answering is left as it is.
5. **Says what is left:** the sessions it could not restart (one answering, the one you
   ran it from, on Windows any of Claude Desktop), and which task each space has active.

For those left, ask the session to park its task, and close and open it. A session that
was open keeps the old program until it restarts; `/clear` is not enough. When the
session you are in is one of them, its start tells you so. Later on,
`augmented-brain session restart --old` restarts the ones that have gone idle, and
`augmented-brain update --no-restart` updates without restarting any.

### Before you update

- **Set up a backup** if you have none: say "set up the backup" to Claude. `augmented-brain
  doctor` says which spaces have none.
- **Update every computer you use.** An older version never breaks notes a newer one
  wrote: it refuses them and asks to be updated.

### When a version changes how notes are stored

Sometimes a new version stores notes in a new way. Then the first session moves them, after
keeping a full copy in the `migrations/` folder of the configuration, and Claude tells
you. Nothing is moved without that copy.

## Uninstalling

```bash
augmented-brain uninstall
```

It shows what it will remove and asks. There are three levels:

| Command | Removes | Keeps |
|---|---|---|
| `uninstall` | The program and the Claude Code plugin | Your notes and the configuration |
| `uninstall --config` | Also the configuration and your profile | Your notes |
| `uninstall --all` | Also every space's notes | Your backups |

- **To come back**, install again: with the configuration there, it finds everything as it
  was; without it, it makes the spaces again over your notes, losing none.
- **`--all` deletes your notes.** It shows each notes folder with how many notes it has,
  and warns about those with no backup: they will be gone for good. Answer no, set up the
  backup or copy the folders, and run it again.
- **Your backups are never deleted**, on GitHub or anywhere. It says which they are and how
  to delete one, if you want to.
- Claude Code, its desktop app and git stay.

On Windows the program file disappears a moment after the command ends: Windows does not
let a running program delete itself.

## Moving to a new computer

1. On the old one, make a last backup: `augmented-brain backup --all`.
2. On the new one, install augmented brain, then restore each space:
   `augmented-brain restore <address of its backup>`.
3. Give again what does not travel: the lists of the guard, and the secrets' values
   (`restore` names those its keychain lacks, with the command to store each).

See [Backup and restore](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html), and [Where everything lives](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/where-things-live.html) for
what travels and what does not.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html

# Commands


Every command of the program, with every option. Day to day you do not need them: you
talk to Claude. They are for setting up, checking and moving to a new machine.

Run them in a terminal. Most act on **the space of the folder you are in**. Outside every
space's folder, they use the default space.

```bash
cd ~/augmented-brain/work
augmented-brain check
```

Options go before or after the other arguments, with one dash or two (`--all` or
`-all`). A command that gets an argument it does not take says so, and does nothing.

Three commands are started by Claude Code, not by you: `mcp`, `hook` and `panel serve`.
They are here so you know what they are.

Inside Claude Code there is one slash command: `/brain:panel` opens the panel, as
`augmented-brain panel` does.

## augmented-brain init

Sets everything up: the spaces, the configuration and the Claude Code plugin. The
installer runs it for you the first time.

```bash
augmented-brain init
```

With no options it asks nothing. It takes the language from the system and creates two
spaces in `~/augmented-brain`: `work` and `personal` (`trabajo` and `personal` in
Spanish), with `personal` as the default space. Then it installs the plugin. Without
Claude Code, it prints the two commands that install the plugin later.

If there is a configuration already, it stops and changes nothing. To add a space, use
`space add`. It writes the configuration last: if it stops half way, run it again.

- `--custom`: ask for the language, the space and its folders, to make one space your way.
- `--language`: the language, `en` or `es`. Without it, the system's (or `AB_LANGUAGE`).
- `--space`: the name of the one space to create (lowercase letters, digits and dashes,
  starting with a letter).
- `--work`: its work folder. Default: `~/augmented-brain/<space>`.
- `--memory`: its notes folder. Default: `notes` inside the work folder.
- `--yes`: do not ask; take the options given and the defaults.
- `--no-plugin`: do not install the Claude Code plugin.

`--space`, `--work` or `--memory` make a single space instead of the two.

```bash
augmented-brain init --space client --work ~/clients/acme --language en
```

## augmented-brain space

Says which space this folder belongs to, and where its notes are.

```bash
augmented-brain space
```

Outside every space's folder it names the default space. With no default space, it says
so, and lists the spaces. It takes no options.

## augmented-brain space add

Adds another space: a client, a side project, a volunteer job.

```bash
augmented-brain space add client
```

The name goes as an argument (first or last) or with `--space`. It asks for the work
folder and the notes folder, suggesting `~/augmented-brain/<name>` and its `notes`
folder. If there was no default space yet, it sets one: `personal` if a space has that
name, or else the space that was there first.

- `--space`: the name of the new space.
- `--work`: its work folder.
- `--memory`: its notes folder.
- `--yes`: do not ask; take the options given and the defaults.

It has no `--language`. The language is the same for every space on this computer: the
`language` setting, which `init` sets. See [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html).

```bash
augmented-brain space add client --work ~/clients/acme --yes
```

See [Spaces](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html).

## augmented-brain check

Checks the notes of this folder's space, and rebuilds its index when they are all valid.

```bash
augmented-brain check
```

It also:

- moves the notes to a new format when a new version needs it, after a full copy;
- checks the shared notes, and rebuilds their index;
- names every file that holds a secret (the backup refuses it until the secret is out);
- names the repositories notes point at that are not on this computer;
- makes the notes readable by you only, if other users could read them;
- moves the list of secret names into `secrets.toml`, from `config.toml` where 0.6.0 kept it;
- moves the oldest journal entries of a task past 24 KB to `archive/journals/`, as the
  tools do when they write it (see [A long journal](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/tasks.html#a-long-journal)).

Run it after editing notes by hand. It ends with an error when a note is not valid. It
takes no options.

## augmented-brain doctor

Says what is missing, and how to fix it.

```bash
augmented-brain doctor
```

Each line starts with a mark: `✓` fine, `·` for your information, `!` a warning, `✗`
something that fails. Under a line that needs work, `→` says what to do. It checks:

- the configuration, the profile and which space this folder is in;
- each space's notes folder, its notes and its index, and whether it has a backup;
- tasks too long to read in one go, which `check` shortens;
- how much of every session start your rules take, with the three longest: they go whole
  to every session, so a shorter rule costs less each time;
- Claude Code, git and the plugin, and whether Claude Code is recent enough to stop
  everything when the guard fails (2.1.295 or later);
- the guard, for real, with a command that must be stopped;
- the guard's lists, the root exceptions in `root_ask`, and those that have ended;
- Claude sessions still running an older version after an update;
- a second memory that Claude Code keeps of its own for your folders;
- notes that other users of the computer could read;
- whether there is a default space, and whether a restore left the guard's lists empty;
- remote access, one line per space, when you set it up with `remote install`: a warning
  when its service is not running, Claude does not trust its folder yet, or (on Linux)
  linger is off;
- how many versions of the configuration are kept, and whether it changed outside them
  (by hand);
- the guard's lists changed since you last accepted them, and a repository both
  untouchable and allowed;
- a Claude window using a lot of memory (2 GB or more);
- the panel from another device, once you have used it: Tailscale, HTTPS, and an address
  left published;
- what working with Claude Code left behind: its worktrees whose session is over, and the
  scratch folders of sessions that ended (see `clean`);
- background sessions that keep their process while nobody uses them: ended or archived,
  or opened by no task and idle for over 12 hours (archiving one in Claude Desktop does
  not stop it), each with the `claude stop` that ends it.

It ends with an error when something fails. When the configuration cannot be read, it
points to `config history` and `config restore`. It takes no options. See
[Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html).

## augmented-brain import

Brings in a memory Claude Code already wrote. Without `--apply` it only shows what it
would do.

```bash
augmented-brain import ~/.claude/projects/<folder>/memory
```

- `--apply`: write the notes. Without it, nothing is written.
- `--map`: a file that says which space each area or note goes to: lines `area-x =
  space`, `task-y = space`, `lesson-z = shared`, and `* = space` for the rest.
- `--repos-base`: the folder the `repos:` paths of the source are relative to.

It never writes over a note that exists, and only reads the source. See
[Bring in a memory](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/import.html).

## augmented-brain backup

Saves the latest changes of this folder's space to its private repository. It also runs
by itself when a Claude session ends.

```bash
augmented-brain backup
```

- `--all`: back up every space, not only this folder's.
- `--space`: back up this space, wherever you are: `--space work`.
- `--auto`: how the end of a session starts it, in the background. Quiet, and it never
  waits for a password. You do not need it.

It stops without pushing when a note holds a secret, or when another machine changed the
same note in another way, and says which. See [Backup and restore](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/backup.html).

## augmented-brain backup setup

Connects this folder's space to a private git repository. It does not copy anything yet:
run `augmented-brain backup` afterwards for the first copy (it says so).

```bash
augmented-brain backup setup git@gitlab.com:lucia/brain-work.git
```

It takes one argument, the repository's address, and no options. To create the
repository in your GitHub account for you, ask Claude: "set up the backup".

## augmented-brain restore

Brings a space back from its backup, on a new machine.

```bash
augmented-brain restore https://github.com/lucia/augmented-brain-work.git
```

It replaces the empty space of the same name with yours. It leaves alone a space that
already has notes. It installs the Claude Code plugin if it is missing. Then it names
what it did not bring: the guard's lists, the repositories where Claude may commit, and
the secrets this machine's keychain lacks, each with the command to store it. When it
cannot ask the keychain (there is none, or it is locked), it names the secrets it could
not check.

- `--memory`: where to put the space's notes. Default: where they were, inside the work
  folder.
- `--work`: the work folder that selects the space. Default: the one saved in the backup.

## augmented-brain panel

Opens the panel in your browser: today at a glance, and every page of your spaces to see
and edit.

```bash
augmented-brain panel
```

It starts the panel in the background, or finds the one running, and opens the browser
on Today, with the space of this folder. It returns at once. The panel stops by itself
after 30 minutes without use. The address it prints opens the panel once, within 2
minutes; run by Claude, with the browser open, it prints none.

- `--no-browser`: only print the address, do not open the browser. `AB_NO_BROWSER=1` does
  the same.

See [The panel](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html).

## augmented-brain panel remote

Opens the panel for your other devices (another computer, your phone), through
[Tailscale](https://tailscale.com), a free app that joins your devices in a private
network of their own.

```bash
augmented-brain panel remote
```

It starts the panel and publishes it in your Tailscale network only. If the panel is
already open, that same panel answers through the network too, so the pages you have
open keep working. It prints the address and a QR code to open it from the phone. Only
your own devices, signed in with the account this computer belongs to, can open it; the address opens it once,
within 10 minutes, and the pages stop working when the panel stops. Whatever is missing (Tailscale itself, HTTPS in your network, letting your
user publish) it explains, with the step to take: it never installs or changes anything
of Tailscale's for you. See [The panel from another device](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel-remote.html).

## augmented-brain panel stop

Stops the panel now.

```bash
augmented-brain panel stop
```

It says whether a panel was running. The link at the bottom of every panel page does the
same.

## augmented-brain panel serve

The panel itself, running in the background. `augmented-brain panel` starts it; you never
run it by hand. It stops on its own after 30 minutes without use.

## augmented-brain remote

Keeps Claude reachable from another computer or your phone, also after a reboot. It is
three commands, `install`, `uninstall` and `status`, each with its own section below.
It uses a `systemd` user service on Linux, a LaunchAgent on macOS and a task of the Task
Scheduler on Windows. On Linux a fourth one, `watch`, is run by a timer, not by you.
Without a subcommand, or with another, `remote` prints its usage.
See [Remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html).

## augmented-brain remote install

Sets remote access up, one service per space.

```bash
augmented-brain remote install
```

For each space named in `remote.toml` (by default, the default space) it writes a service
that runs `claude remote-control` in the space's first work folder (or the one `folders`
names in `remote.toml`), and starts it: a `systemd` user service on Linux, a LaunchAgent
in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` on macOS, a task `\augmented-brain\remote-<space>` of the
Task Scheduler on Windows (it runs while you are logged in, with no window). Only a space with no work
folder gets a folder of its own, `remote/<space>` in the configuration folder, which
becomes its work folder. It needs `claude` (on your PATH, or where its installer puts it)
and a folder that exists. The service gets a PATH with the folders of `claude` and
`augmented-brain`, so its sessions find both after a reboot. You can run it again at any
time: it changes only what is different.

On Linux it also installs the watch: a `systemd` timer, `augmented-brain-watch-remote`,
that runs `augmented-brain remote watch` every two minutes (see below).

It then says what is still missing, and does none of it for you:

- Claude must **trust each folder**. It prints `cd <folder> && claude` for each one that
  is not trusted yet (on Windows, `cd "<folder>"; claude`): run it once and accept the
  question.
- On Linux, **linger** must be on for the services to start after a reboot with nobody
  logged in. It prints the command, `sudo loginctl enable-linger <you>`, for you to run.
  macOS and Windows have no linger: the service starts when you log in.

Without systemd's user services (a container, or WSL without systemd), launchctl on macOS
or the Task Scheduler on Windows, it says so and changes nothing. It takes no options. The settings are in `remote.toml` (see [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html)).

## augmented-brain remote uninstall

Stops remote access and removes it.

```bash
augmented-brain remote uninstall
```

It stops and removes the services `remote install` wrote (on Linux, the watch first), and sets `enabled = false` in
`remote.toml`. The folders and their entries in `work_folders` stay: it never deletes
anything else. It takes no options.

## augmented-brain remote status

Says how remote access stands, and changes nothing.

```bash
augmented-brain remote status
```

For each space: the session's name (what you pick in Claude Desktop or claude.ai), whether
the service is running and starts by itself, and whether Claude trusts its folder. Then,
on Linux, whether the watch (see `remote watch` below) is running and how long ago it last
looked, and whether linger is on; on macOS and Windows, that it starts when you log in. Under each problem, `→` says what to do. It takes no options.

## augmented-brain remote watch

Brings a service back when the server archived its session. Linux only. Its timer runs
it every two minutes; you do not need to.

```bash
augmented-brain remote watch
```

A healthy `claude remote-control` keeps a Claude process for its session. When the server
archives the session (for example, you archived it in claude.ai), that process ends and
the service goes on running with no session: nobody can connect, and systemd sees nothing
wrong. The watch notices a service with no session at two looks in a row and restarts it.
If it still has none after that, Claude was trying to reopen the archived session: the
watch renames Claude's record of it (`bridge-pointer.json` becomes
`bridge-pointer.json.archived`, in the folder's project in `~/.claude/projects`) and
restarts it again, so a new session starts, in about three minutes. The conversation of
the archived session does not come back. What it does goes to the system journal
(`journalctl --user -u augmented-brain-watch-remote`). It takes no options.

On every look it also keeps your task sessions safe. Stopping a service stops everything
started inside it, and a session of a task started from a remote session (with
`augmented-brain session start`, or `claude --bg`) can start Claude's background service
there, which runs every task session. So the watch moves out of each service whatever
its server did not start itself (Claude's background service, its sessions, anything
else a session left running) into a group of its own, `augmented-brain-kept-<number>`.
`remote install` and `remote uninstall` do the same before they restart or stop a
service; when it cannot be done, they stop and say so, and the watch does not restart
that service.

## augmented-brain session

Opens a remote session of its own for one task, so that from another computer you can
work on several tasks at once, each in its own session. It is four commands, `start`,
`stop`, `restart` and `list`, each with its own section below; `restart` also restarts
the other Claude sessions on this computer. Linux only for now: it has
been tried only there. Without a subcommand, or with another, `session` prints its usage. See
[Remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html#a-session-per-task).

## augmented-brain session start

Opens a session for a task, in the task's folder.

```bash
augmented-brain session start task-new-website
augmented-brain session start task-new-website --folder ~/projects/website
```

It starts a background Claude session of its own for the task (`claude --bg
--remote-control`), named after the task's title. Within a minute it shows up in Claude
Desktop and claude.ai. It starts on its own: its first message has it read its task,
tell you where it stands, and get on with the next step. When another Claude session
asked for it, the first message also has it tell that session, in one line, when it
stops: the task closed or parked, or waiting on you. Since you see what a background
session writes only when you open it, it also sends you a notification then (on the
desktop and, with Remote Control, on your phone), and when something it watched ends.
The folder is the first of the task's repositories found in the space's work folders,
or the one `--folder` gives. A task that names no repository opens in the space's first
work folder, which several such tasks may share.

A bare repository has no files to work on, so the task gets a git worktree of its own
next to it: `site-new-website` for the task `task-new-website` of `site`, on a new branch
named after the task, from the default branch of origin as it is now (it fetches first).
Two tasks of one repository never share a folder, and a session never starts on old
code. Asked again, it uses the same worktree. The same goes for a bare repository given
with `--folder`. A folder given with `--folder` must lie inside the work folders of the
task's space: a session elsewhere would not find its task. On a system where task
sessions do not run yet, the command says so before it makes anything.

Run it from a folder of the task's space: the remote
session you reach from another computer can run it for you ("open me a session for
the website task"). Every session on Linux knows how.

Two rules keep it safe. The folder must be trusted on its own: trusting a folder above
it is not enough, so the first time the command says to open Claude once in that folder
and accept the question. Claude itself would not ask, and a repository's own settings
and hooks must not run unasked. A git worktree is the exception: Claude keeps the answer
under its main repository, so trusting either one is enough. And one task per folder:
two tasks in one folder would step on each other's changes, so a folder another task's
session uses is refused; give it another with `--folder` (a git worktree, for example).

It waits for the session's first answer, up to a minute, and returns as soon as it
comes. A session that cannot work is not left behind: when Claude Code is not logged
in, or its login has expired, nothing is opened, and when the first answer is an error
(the login ran out, the service is overloaded), the session is closed. Either way the
command says what happened and what to do, such as logging in again with `claude auth
login`.

If Claude stopped the task's session (it does that to one left unused for hours, and
to every one when its background service restarts), `session start` brings it back
instead: the same session, with its whole conversation, connected again in Claude
Desktop and claude.ai, and no new first message. claude.ai shows such a session as
disconnected and cannot bring it back by itself. Only if Claude refuses does a new
session open and replace it.

The session closes with `session stop`, or when the computer restarts. Launched
sessions are not brought back after a reboot: ask for them again.

## augmented-brain session stop

Closes a task's session and takes it out of Claude Desktop and claude.ai. It works
from any folder.

```bash
augmented-brain session stop task-new-website
```

When `session start` made a worktree for the task, `stop` also removes it with its
branch, as long as nothing would be lost: with changes not committed (files git does not
show by your settings count too), commits not pushed (on the task's branch, even when the
worktree was left on another commit), or files git ignores that no build makes again (a
`.env`, a key; `node_modules`, `build`, `dist` and the like do not count), it keeps it and
says so. Closing the task closes its session too, once it has finished its answer,
worktree and all. Sessions that end without `stop` (a reboot, a session closed from Claude
Desktop) leave theirs: the next `session start` removes those with nothing of their own
(not one made in the last ten minutes, whose session may still be starting), closing the
task removes its own, and `doctor` only looks: it says how many would go and warns about
any that stays with work in it.

If Claude cannot tell whether the session still runs (its list cannot be read), `stop`
says so and changes nothing: the session stays on record and its worktree stays too.

A session Claude retired (it does that to one left unused for hours) is closed too.
Claude's background service may have stopped by then; `stop` starts it for a moment,
and it goes away by itself. If Claude still cannot take the session out of its lists,
`stop` says so and gives the command to do it later. A task with no session gets
"nothing to close", never a silent success.

- `--when-idle`: wait until the session has finished its answer, then close it. Closing
  the task runs it by itself in the background: the session closing its own task is
  often still answering, and stopping it there would cut that answer off. A session can
  also close itself this way: the command returns at once, and a process in the
  background does the waiting. A session waiting for a permission counts as answering.
  It waits up to 30 minutes; one still answering by then stays open. What it did goes to
  `state/session-stop.log` in the configuration folder.

## augmented-brain session restart

Restarts a Claude session so it uses the program of now, with the same conversation.
It works from any folder. Use it after an update, or right after parking a task, so
that its session starts afresh.

```bash
augmented-brain session restart task-new-website
augmented-brain session restart --old
```

The session is named by its task (when `session start` opened it), its id, the first
eight characters of its session id, or its name; `claude agents` lists them. Each kind
restarts its own way:

- **A task's session** (`claude --bg`): Claude gives it a new process with the same
  conversation. One you archived, or that ended, is never brought back: only its
  augmented brain server stops, and it starts again, of now, if you ever open it.
- **A session of the remote access** (`remote install`): its service restarts, and the
  same session comes back in claude.ai and Claude Desktop in about ten seconds. The
  service holds every session it serves, so it restarts only when all of them are
  idle. Anything else inside the service (Claude's background service, above all) is
  moved out first, so it does not stop with it. Linux only.
- **A session of Claude Desktop or a terminal:** its window stays open. Its app opened
  it, and stopping it from outside would break that window, so only its augmented
  brain server stops; Claude Code starts it again, from the program of now, the next
  time the session uses it. Linux and macOS. On Windows it is left as it is: close it
  and open it again yourself.

A session that is answering, or waiting for a permission, is never restarted: it is
looked at again right before, and left as it is if it is not idle. Nor is the session
the command runs in: that one needs `--when-idle`. One that fails leaves the others
going.

- `--old`: restart every idle session still running an earlier augmented brain, one at
  a time, and say what happened to each. `update` runs it by itself. Here only a
  task's own session (opened by `session start`) is brought back: any other background
  session may have been archived in Claude Desktop, which Claude is not told, so only
  its augmented brain server stops.
- `--when-idle`: wait until the session has finished its answer, then restart it. This
  is how a session restarts itself after parking its task: the command returns at
  once, and a process in the background waits, up to 30 minutes. What it did goes to
  `state/session-restart.log` in the configuration folder.

## augmented-brain session list

Lists the task sessions open on this computer: the task, whether it runs, and its
folder. **retired** means Claude stopped it, after hours unused or when its background
service restarted: claude.ai shows it as disconnected, and `session start` with its task
brings it back with its whole conversation. **failed** means its last
answer was an error, such as an expired login: it does nothing until someone writes to
it. The line gives the error and what to do.

```bash
augmented-brain session list
```

## augmented-brain watch

Follows something that takes a while and says how it ended, so a session can leave it
running and get on with other work. For now it follows one thing, a pull request: see
`watch pr` below. Without a subcommand, `watch` prints its usage.

## augmented-brain watch pr

Follows a pull request on GitHub until there is something to tell: it is merged or
closed, it conflicts with its base branch (no CI runs then), a required check fails, every required check has finished, or `--max` passes.
Then it ends on its own and says how it went, in one line.

```bash
augmented-brain watch pr 104 --task task-my-change
```

- `--task TASK` writes that line in the task's journal (with the next step the task
  had), and what happened, in a sentence of the program's own, as its next step: the
  names of the checks are chosen by whoever writes the pull request's workflows, so
