  they go only in the journal, never in what every session reads at the start. Every other session hears of it before its next
  answer, and the panel's Today shows it. The watching is then done by a process of
  its own, which goes on if the session that started it is closed, restarted or
  retired by Claude: the session only waits for its result. Asked again for the same
  pull request and task, it waits for the one already running instead of starting
  another. The task must be in this folder's space.
- `--repo OWNER/NAME` is the repository; by default, the one of this folder.
- `--max` is the longest it watches (3h by default); `--every` how often it looks
  (30s by default, 10s at least).

The checks that are not required do not decide anything, but the line names those
still running or failed: each name between quotes, on one line and cut at 60
characters, five at most. It never waits for ever: if GitHub lists no required check
after 5 minutes, or gh fails three times in a row or gives an answer it does not
understand, it stops and says what gh said. It needs `gh` with your GitHub login. The
assistant runs it in the background; its last line asks it to tell you straight away.
It ends with 0 when the checks passed or the pull request was merged, and 1 otherwise.

## augmented-brain config

The versions of your configuration: two commands, `history` and `restore`, each with its
own section below. Without a subcommand, `config` prints its usage. See
[Configuration versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html).

## augmented-brain config history

Lists the last versions of your configuration, newest first, and changes nothing.

```bash
augmented-brain config history
augmented-brain config history 3
```

A version is a copy of `config.toml`, `guard.toml`, `remote.toml`, `session.toml`,
`profile.md` and `secrets.toml` as they were at one moment, with who changed them: the
panel, a command, the assistant (and which tool), going back to a version, or by hand.
The last 10 are kept, only on this computer. With a number, it shows what that version
changed from the one before it, line by line. It takes no options.

## augmented-brain config restore

Goes back to one version of the configuration.

```bash
augmented-brain config restore 3
```

It shows what changes and writes it. The configuration you had is kept as a version
first, so going back can be undone the same way. A version that would leave a file the
program cannot read is refused, and nothing changes. If the guard's lists end up
different from the ones you accepted, the guard asks before every commit, push or merge
it used to allow. It keeps asking until you accept the lists in the panel's Guard page,
or start a new session. A command can be run by the assistant, so it never accepts them
for you. Going back from
the panel's Versions page does accept them. It works even when `config.toml` is broken,
like `config history`. It takes no options.

## augmented-brain clean

Removes what working with Claude Code leaves behind and nobody cleans up. It shows the
list first, and removes it only if you say yes.

```bash
augmented-brain clean
```

It looks in every folder Claude Code was opened in, and in its scratch folder:

- **Worktrees Claude Code made** (a worktree is a second working copy of a repository; Claude
  Code puts them in `.claude/worktrees`) whose session is over. One goes only when it has no
  change not committed, no commit that is not on the remote, and no file git ignores that
  no build makes again (a `.env`, a key): it is removed with
  `git worktree remove`, never by deleting the folder. Its branch goes with it when Claude
  Code named it (`worktree-<name>`); a branch of yours stays. A worktree with work of its
  own is only named, so you look at it.
- **Worktrees git remembers whose folder is gone**: `git worktree prune` forgets them. Their
  branches stay.
- **Scratch folders of sessions that ended** (`/tmp/claude-<number>` on Linux), untouched for
  over a day. Those of running sessions stay, and so does anything else there.

Before removing each thing it looks again, so a session that started meanwhile keeps its
folders. `doctor` says when there is something to clean.

- `--yes`: do not ask.

## augmented-brain update

Updates augmented brain and its Claude Code plugin.

```bash
augmented-brain update
```

If there is a newer version, it runs the published installer, which replaces the program
and then updates the plugin. If not, it only updates the plugin. It first asks GitHub
for the latest version, once: if GitHub does not answer, it says so and stops. If the
download of the installer fails (three tries, also through GitHub's API) or the program is not the new version
afterwards, it says so, ends with an error and changes nothing. The installer tries the
new program before it replaces the old one: if it does not start, the old one stays and
`update` ends with an error. Around a new version it
does what you would otherwise do by hand:

- **Before:** the health check of `doctor` (what fails is shown, so it is not taken
  for a problem of the new version), and a backup of every space that has one. If a
  backup fails, it stops and updates nothing: that copy is the way back. With no backup
  at all, it says it goes ahead without a copy to go back to.
- **After:** the idle Claude sessions still running the old version are restarted,
  one at a time, as `session restart --old` does: those of Claude Desktop stay open and
  only their augmented brain restarts. For those it cannot restart (one answering, or
  on Windows one of Claude Desktop), it says which task is active in each space, so you
  ask its session to park it, and then you close and open them.

- `--plugin`: update only the Claude Code plugin. The installer uses it.
- `--force`: update even when the backup before it fails.
- `--no-restart`: restart no session after updating; it only says which still run the
  old version.
- `--from <address>`: for tests: install the release at this address instead of
  GitHub's latest. It must be `https://`, `file://`, or `http://` to this computer or to
  the host of a test VM (`10.0.2.2`).

`update` ignores `AB_RELEASE_URL` and `AB_MARKETPLACE`, and says so: a program could set
them so that the update comes from somewhere else. Of the other `AB_` variables, it only
passes `AB_CONFIG_DIR` and `AB_INSTALL_DIR` on to the installer.

## augmented-brain uninstall

Removes the program and the Claude Code plugin. Your notes stay.

```bash
augmented-brain uninstall
```

It shows what it will remove and asks first. The remote access services and the
sessions opened for tasks go first; if one cannot be stopped, nothing else is removed.

- `--config`: also remove the configuration and the profile.
- `--all`: start from scratch: also the configuration, the profile and every space's
  notes. It shows each notes folder with how many notes it has, and warns about those
  with no backup, which will be gone for good. Only what augmented brain keeps in a notes
  folder goes; a folder that holds a work folder, or has no notes, stays whole. Your
  backups are not touched.
- `--yes`: do not ask.

See [Installing](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/install.html#uninstalling).

## augmented-brain mcp

Runs the MCP server: the tools Claude uses to keep your tasks and notes. **Claude Code
starts it**, through the plugin; you do not.

It talks over its input and output. It finds the space again on every call, from the
folder Claude works in. The tools are in [MCP tools](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html). It takes no options.

## augmented-brain hook

Answers a Claude Code hook: a call Claude Code makes at a given moment. **Claude Code
runs it**, through the plugin; you do not. It reads what Claude Code sends on its input,
and never makes Claude fail: a problem goes to its error output.

```bash
augmented-brain hook session-start 1
```

The events:

- `session-start`: a session starts. It hands Claude the profile, the rules, the index of
  tasks and what is due. It comes in up to nine parts, `session-start 1` to
  `session-start 9`, because Claude Code cuts each hook's text at 10,000 characters. Only
  the parts with something in them are sent.
- `pre-tool-use`: before every command and file change. This is the
  [guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html). If it cannot run, Claude Code stops the command.
- `user-prompt-submit`: before Claude answers a message. It tells Claude which tasks
  changed outside its session since it last looked (another session closed one, the
  panel changed its next step), so it reads them again instead of trusting what it read
  earlier. It never holds up the message.
- `stop`: after each answer. It reminds Claude to write in the journal of its session's
  task, once, after 20 minutes without writing. It also looks at how much memory the window uses
  (VS Code's extension host, or Claude itself in a terminal), and has Claude warn you
  when it passes 2 GB, then 4 and 8 GB, once each. On Linux and macOS; it takes a
  fraction of a millisecond. See
  [Troubleshooting](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/troubleshooting.html#the-window-uses-a-lot-of-memory).
- `post-compact`: after Claude Code compacts a long conversation. It keeps the summary in
  `archive/sessions/` and points the task's journal at it.
- `session-end`: the session ends. It notes that it ended well, and starts the backup in
  the background.

## augmented-brain version

Prints the version of the program.

```bash
augmented-brain version
```

`--version` and `-v` do the same.

## augmented-brain help

Prints the list of commands, in your language.

```bash
augmented-brain help
```

`--help` and `-h` do the same. Running `augmented-brain` with nothing prints the list
too, as an error (exit code 2).


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html

# MCP tools


You say "park it". Claude calls the tool `task_park`, with the task's id and the next
step. The program writes the task file. You never call these tools yourself: Claude does,
behind your words.

**MCP** (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard to give tools to an assistant. The
program serves these tools with `augmented-brain mcp`, which Claude Code starts through
the plugin. In Claude Code they show up as `mcp__plugin_brain_augmented-brain__<tool>`.

A few things hold for every tool:

- It works on **the space of the folder Claude is in**, found again on every call.
- Tools run one at a time, and wait for the panel, so two never write at once.
- **No secrets.** A tool refuses to write a password, a token or a key into a note.
- **Nothing is deleted.** Tasks are closed, not removed.
- **Titles, summaries, next steps and names are one line.** Line breaks in them become
  spaces, so text copied from outside can never open a section of its own in what
  every session reads at the start. Each field has a generous limit (a next step, 2,000
  characters; a journal entry, 32,000): past it, nothing is saved and the error says
  where the long text goes. The [memory format](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html#file-header)
  lists them all.
- Dates are written `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- A parameter is required unless it says optional.

## Tools by purpose

- **Where things are**: [`where_am_i`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#where_am_i), [`pending`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#pending).
- **Tasks**: [`task_new`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_new), [`task_get`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_get),
  [`task_update`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_update), [`task_step`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_step),
  [`task_journal`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_journal), [`task_park`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_park), [`task_close`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_close),
  [`task_worktree`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#task_worktree).
- **Inbox and the weekly review**: [`capture`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#capture),
  [`capture_done`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#capture_done), [`weekly_review`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#weekly_review), [`review_done`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#review_done).
- **Notes that last**: [`area_new`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#area_new), [`knowledge_new`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#knowledge_new),
  [`rule_new`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#rule_new), [`note_retire`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#note_retire), [`person_save`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#person_save),
  [`repo_describe`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#repo_describe).
- **You and this machine**: [`profile_save`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#profile_save),
  [`safety_save`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#safety_save), [`secret_name_save`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#secret_name_save),
  [`backup_setup`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#backup_setup), [`session_recover`](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html#session_recover).

## `where_am_i`

Which space this session works in, its notes folder, its areas, and how many tasks are
live. It takes no parameters.

## `pending`

The live tasks, those waiting on you first, each with its status, steps done, who it
waits on and its next step (cut at 300 characters: `task_get` gives it whole). Then the
watch dates that are due. Claude uses it for "where were we?".

- `within_days` (optional): also list watch dates due within this many days. Default 7.
- `space` (optional): another of your spaces, to list its live tasks instead, read
  only: to find the task you mean there.

## `task_new`

Opens a new task, in the definition phase and waiting on you. With a parent, it is a
subtask.

- `title`: a short name for the task.
- `summary` (optional): one line on what it is.
- `area` (optional): the id of its area. Default: the parent's area, or `area-general`.
- `parent` (optional): the id of the task this one is a part of. One level only: the
  parent cannot be a subtask, nor closed.
- `goal` (optional): one line on what the task is for. It goes into the Definition.
- `done_when` (optional): one line on how we will know it worked. It goes into the
  Definition.

## `task_get`

Reads a task: its header, its whole body with the journal, and its subtasks. It also says
which task it is part of, and whether a repository it names is missing from this
computer. Claude reads a task before resuming it. Old journal entries moved to
`archive/journals/` are named by a line of the journal (see
[A long journal](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/tasks.html#a-long-journal)); a task still too long for one answer, written
by hand or by an earlier version, is read without its oldest entries, and a line says
where they are.

- `id`: the task's id, such as `task-move-the-blog`.
- `space` (optional): another of your spaces, whose task this is. Claude uses it only
  when you ask to work on a task of that space from here. See
  [A task of another space](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html#a-task-of-another-space).

## `task_update`

Changes a task. Only the fields given change. A change of status is written in the
journal, and when it skips phases (straight from `definition` to `execution`, say), the
line names the ones skipped: skipping is allowed, and it is seen. A closed task opens
again only with `reopen`.

- `id`: the task's id.
- `status` (optional): `definition`, `analysis`, `plan`, `execution`, `validation`,
  `closed`, `parked` or `someday`.
- `waiting_on` (optional): `me`, `nobody`, a person, or another task's id.
- `next` (optional): the single next action, in one line.
- `summary` (optional): one line on what it is.
- `area` (optional): the id of its area.
- `watch_date` (optional): add a date to look at something again. Needs `watch_what`.
- `watch_what` (optional): what to look at on `watch_date`, in one line.
- `watch_done` (optional): mark the watch date of this day as done.
- `reopen` (optional): only to open a closed task again, with a new `status`: why, in a
  few words. It goes to the journal. Claude asks you first.
- `space` (optional): another of your spaces, whose task this is. Claude uses it only
  when you ask to work on a task of that space from here. Closing it is left to a
  session of that space. See
  [A task of another space](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html#a-task-of-another-space).

At least one field besides `id` and `space` is needed.

## `task_step`

Steps are the small parts of a task: checkboxes (`- [ ] text`) in its Plan. This tool adds
one, or ticks or unticks one. Each change writes a short journal line, and the answer
lists the steps. A closed task's steps stay as they were closed.

- `id`: the task's id.
- `add` (optional): add this step, unticked, at the end of the Plan, instead of ticking
  one.
- `number` (optional): the step to tick or untick, 1 for the first checkbox.
- `text` (optional): the step to tick or untick, by its text (or a part only it holds),
  when `number` is not given.
- `done` (optional): `true` to tick the step, `false` to untick it. Left out, it unticks.
- `space` (optional): another of your spaces, whose task this is. Claude uses it only
  when you ask to work on a task of that space from here. See
  [A task of another space](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html#a-task-of-another-space).

## `task_journal`

Adds a dated entry to a task's journal. Claude writes one at the moment something is
done or decided.

- `id`: the task's id.
- `entry`: what was done, what came out, what was decided.
- `space` (optional): another of your spaces, whose task this is. Claude uses it only
  when you ask to work on a task of that space from here. The entry ends in
  `(from <this space>)`. See
  [A task of another space](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html#a-task-of-another-space).

## `task_park`

Pauses a task without losing anything, before switching to other work. A closed task is
refused: it opens again only with `task_update` and `reopen`, so its result stays.

- `id`: the task's id.
- `next`: exactly how to resume: a command, a file or a decision.
- `waiting_on` (optional): who it waits on now.
- `essentials` (optional, but Claude should pass it): three to six lines that are enough to
  resume without the journal. They replace the task's first section. Without it, only
  "where it is" and "next" are updated there.
- `someday` (optional): `true` when it will not be touched for weeks. The task leaves
  the daily list.

## `task_close`

Closes a finished task with its result. It is kept, never deleted. A task with open
subtasks cannot close, and a task already closed is refused, so its result is never
written over. If the task has watch dates not marked done, it says so: they
still come up at the start of the session on their day, since closing is often when you
write down what to check later. When `session start` made a git worktree for the task and
its session no longer runs, closing removes it with its branch if it holds nothing that
is not on the remote (nor a file git ignores that no build makes again, such as a
`.env`), and says so; otherwise it says why it stays. When the task's own
session still runs (often the one closing it), a process of its own closes that session
once it has finished its answer, takes it out of Claude Desktop and claude.ai, and
removes its worktree the same way. A session Claude retired after hours unused answers
nothing: it is closed at once.

- `id`: the task's id.
- `result`: what was achieved, in one or two lines.

## `task_worktree`

Makes a git worktree for a task, or notes one already made, so closing the task removes
it. A worktree is a second folder of a repository, on a branch of its own, so a task can
change code without touching the main folder. Made here, it is `<repo>-<task>`, next to
the repository, on a new branch named after the task, from origin's default branch as it
is now; asked again, it returns the same one. When the task is closed, each noted
worktree with nothing not committed, nothing not pushed and no ignored file of its own
(a `.env`) is removed, with the branch
made for it (a noted one keeps its branch); one with work of its own stays, and so does
the one the closing session works in, and the answer says why. Both paths must lie
inside the space's work folders.

- `id`: the task's id.
- `repo` (optional): a git repository: makes the task's worktree of it.
- `folder` (optional): a worktree already made for the task: notes it. Give `repo` or
  `folder`, one of the two.

## `capture`

Notes something in the inbox without opening a task, optionally with a day to be
reminded. The weekly review processes it.

- `text`: the idea, link or loose end, in one line.
- `remind_on` (optional): a date. It comes up at the start of the session from a week
  before, until it is dealt with.
- `space` (optional): another of your spaces, to send it there instead. It lands in
  that space's inbox marked with where it came from, `(from personal)`, and comes up at
  the start of every session there until it is done. For something decided in one space
  that has to be done in another. Claude only does it when you ask: what goes to a
  space is seen there and goes into its backup.

## `capture_done`

Takes one capture out of the inbox once it is done, or once it has become a task,
without waiting for the weekly review. Above all for what another space sent, which
otherwise comes up at every session start.

- `date`: the day it was captured, as listed.
- `text`: its text exactly as listed, with or without its origin. Another capture with
  the same text stays.

## `weekly_review`

Lists what the weekly review goes through: the inbox, live tasks untouched for 14 days
or more, and the dates due in the next 7 days. Claude then goes through it with you, one
item at a time. It takes no parameters.

## `review_done`

Finishes the weekly review. It saves what was decided in `reviews/`, with the captures
it takes out of the inbox (each with its date), and only then takes them out. A review
that cannot be saved (an empty summary, something that looks like a secret) leaves the
inbox as it was, so no capture is lost.

- `summary`: what was decided, in a few lines.
- `processed` (optional): the text of each capture dealt with, exactly as `weekly_review`
  listed it. They leave the inbox. One that is not found is left as it was, and named.

## `area_new`

Creates an area: a responsibility with no end date that groups tasks and knowledge.

- `title`: the area's name.
- `summary` (optional): one line on what it looks after.

## `knowledge_new`

Saves a reference or a lesson worth keeping beyond one task: in this space, or shared by
every space. A title that already exists creates nothing: Claude is told its id, to change
that one or choose another title. Nothing is ever saved twice without anyone knowing.

- `id` (optional): to change a reference or lesson that exists. What is sent replaces
  what it had, what is left out stays, and the version it replaces is kept in
  `archive/`.
- `kind`: `reference` (how something works) or `lesson` (what was learned).
- `title`: for a lesson, a title that already states the conclusion.
- `summary` (optional): one line.
- `area` (optional): the id of its area.
- `body` (optional): the text, in Markdown.
- `shared` (optional): `true` when it holds in every space. It then has no area.

## `rule_new`

Saves a rule you give on how to work. Every session loads it. A title that already exists
creates nothing: Claude is told its id. Claude Code tells you, once, which rule was saved
or changed, in a message of its own at the end of the answer: if you did not ask for it,
tell Claude to undo it.

- `id` (optional): to change a rule that exists. What is sent replaces what it had, what
  is left out stays, and the version it replaces is kept in `archive/`.
- `title`: the rule in a few words.
- `summary` (optional): one line that says what to do.
- `body`: what to do, and why, in Markdown.
- `shared` (optional): `true` when it applies in every space, not only this one.

## `note_retire`

Retires a rule, reference or lesson that no longer holds, without deleting it. It moves
to `archive/`, which is never loaded, so a retired rule stops reaching the session start.
A line at its end says when, why and what replaces it. For a duplicate or an old
version; Claude asks you first. When it retires a rule, Claude Code tells you, once.

- `id`: the rule, reference or lesson.
- `reason`: why, in a few words. It stays with the note.
- `replaced_by` (optional): the id of the note that replaces it.
- `shared` (optional): `true` when the note is in the shared layer.

## `person_save`

Remembers someone you work or deal with, so a first name leads to the right person.
Saving a name that exists updates that person.

A person can be in several spaces: the same person, with the role and notes each space
may show. Claude asks you where it should be visible (for instance, a note about a friend
should not land in your work space) and passes your answer in `spaces`. With only one
space, there is nothing to ask. Without `spaces` and with several, nothing is saved: the
answer lists your spaces and asks. What is saved in a space is seen in that space only.

- `name`: the full name, or how you know them.
- `aliases` (optional): other names you use for them, such as a nickname.
- `role` (optional): who they are to you, in a few words: "my manager", "runs the
  hosting company".
- `notes` (optional): anything else worth remembering.
- `spaces` (optional with one space, needed with several): the names of the spaces where
  this is visible. The role, other names and notes are written in those spaces only.

## `repo_describe`

Writes down, in one line, what one of your git repositories is, for the panel's
Repositories page. Only repositories inside this space's work folders. The line goes to
the reference `ref-repositories`, one line per repository; a new one replaces the old.

- `repo`: the repository: its path (`~/…` or absolute), or its name as a task's `repos:`
  writes it, relative to a work folder.
- `text`: what it is, in one line, in your words. Empty takes the line out.

## `profile_save`

Saves who you are, how you like to work, and the name and personality you give Claude.
Every space shares it, and every session starts by reading it. Claude sends only the
parts that change: a part left out keeps what it has, and an empty one is cleared.
Claude Code tells you, once, which parts changed.

- `name` (needed the first time): what you want to be called.
- `about` (optional): what you do and work on, in short lines starting with `- `.
- `work_style` (optional): how you like to work with Claude: language, length of
  answers, how much to ask before acting. Short lines starting with `- `.
- `assistant_name` (optional): the name you give Claude. It signs with it the emails it
  writes in your name, always followed by a line that says it is an AI (see
  [Panel, Profile](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/panel.html#profile)).
- `assistant_personality` (optional): how you want Claude to be, in your words. Style
  only: it never changes the rules, the guard or its honesty.

## `safety_save`

Adds to what the guard asks you about. The lists hold on this whole machine, in every
space. It only adds: to take one out, you edit the configuration yourself, and the
answer says where. Claude Code tells you, once, what was added.

- `production_aws_profiles` (optional): AWS CLI profiles that reach production. The guard
  asks before commands that use them.
- `untouchable_hosts` (optional): machines not to touch without asking, as you type them
  for ssh.

## `secret_name_save`

Writes down the name of a secret you keep in the system keychain, and what it is for.
Never its value: a value is refused. That covers the tokens of known services, a long
run of letters and digits, a password said with its label (`password=…`, "the password
is …"), an address with a password in it, a JWT and a PIN or CVV with its number. The
list is the same in every space; the panel shows it. Saving a name that is listed changes
what it is for.

- `service`: the service the secret is kept under in the keychain, such as `telegram`.
- `name`: its name under that service, such as `alerts-bot`.
- `what` (optional): what it is for, in a few words: 160 characters at most.

## `backup_setup`

Sets up the backup of this space: a private git repository that keeps its notes, pushed
by itself every time a session ends.

It creates `augmented-brain-<space>`, a private repository in your GitHub account, with
the `gh` command line, and makes the first copy right away. When `gh` is missing or not
logged in, it returns the steps to guide you through.

- `repo_url`: refused. A backup somewhere else (GitLab, your company's git) is yours to
  set up, with `augmented-brain backup setup <url>` or the panel's Backup page: an
  address Claude passes on could come from anything it read, and one call would send
  every note there.

If the space already has a backup, it says where it goes and how the last one went; it
never moves it elsewhere: only you do, with `augmented-brain backup setup <url>`.

## `session_recover`

Reads what you and Claude said in an earlier session of this space that did not end
well, after the last journal entry of its task. Only the messages, no tool output, at
most the last 20,000 characters, from Claude Code's record on this computer (kept 30
days). Claude then writes in the journal what is missing.

- `session_id` (optional): the session to recover. Without it, the one the session start
  offered.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html

# Configuration


The installer writes the configuration for you, and Claude adds to it when you ask
("`shop-prod` is production"). You only open it to change something by hand: a new work
folder, a repository where Claude may commit, a root exception.

## Where it is

One folder per computer, the **configuration folder**:

- Linux and macOS: `~/.config/augmented-brain/` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/augmented-brain/`).
- Windows: `%APPDATA%\augmented-brain\`.
- Anywhere else, if you set `AB_CONFIG_DIR`.

Inside it, `config.toml` holds the settings. It is a **TOML** file: `name = value` lines,
and a `[section]` heading for each space. Lines starting with `#` are comments; the
program keeps them when it changes the file.

## An example

```toml
# ~/.config/augmented-brain/config.toml
language = "en"
default_space = "personal"
production_aws_profiles = ["shop-prod", "shop-prod-eu"]
untouchable_hosts = ["db01", "backup.example.com"]
root_ask = ["web02 until 2026-12-31"]

[spaces.work]
memory = "~/augmented-brain/work/notes"
work_folders = ["~/augmented-brain/work", "~/code"]
backup = "git@gitlab.com:lucia/brain-work.git"
git_allowed_repos = ["~/code/blog", "~/code/blog-*"]
git_ask_repos = ["~/code/shop"]

[spaces.personal]
memory = "~/augmented-brain/personal/notes"
work_folders = ["~/augmented-brain/personal"]
backup = "https://github.com/lucia/augmented-brain-personal.git"
```

Paths may start with `~`, your home folder. The program reads the file every time it
runs, so a change counts at once.

## Settings for the whole computer

These go at the top, before any `[spaces.…]` heading.

- `language`: the language the program speaks to you, `en` or `es`: its messages and the
  guard's reasons. Default `en`.
- `default_space`: the space used outside every work folder, such as the scratch folder
  the desktop app opens a new session in. Its backup carries your profile and the shared
  notes. Optional; with two spaces or more, `init` and `space add` set it.
- `production_aws_profiles`: AWS profiles that reach production. The guard asks you
  before any command that uses one, in every space. See [The guard](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/guard.html).
- `untouchable_hosts`: machines not to touch without asking. The guard asks before
  `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync`, `sftp` and `mosh` to them, in every space. Names match ignoring
  case, and a short name matches the full one (`db01` and `db01.example.com`).
- `root_ask`: temporary exceptions for root, one machine each, written `"<host> until
  <date>"`. The date is a day (`2026-12-31`, which lasts to its end, in UTC) or a time
  (`2026-12-31T23:59Z`). Until then, root on that machine asks you instead of being
  stopped. The date is required.
- `format`: the version of the configuration folder. The program writes it when a new
  version needs it; never change it by hand. Without it, it is 1.

## Settings of each space

Each space is a section, `[spaces.<name>]`. Together they are the `spaces` of the file.
The name is lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter.

- `memory`: the space's notes folder. Required.
- `work_folders`: the folders that pick this space when you open Claude in them, or in a
  folder inside them. See [Spaces](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/spaces.html).
- `backup`: the address of the space's private git repository. `backup setup` writes it.
  Without it, the space is not backed up.
- `git_allowed_repos`: repositories where Claude may commit and push, written with
  `git -C <repo>`. The last part of a path may hold a `*`, which matches one folder. A git
  worktree of a listed repository counts as it.
- `git_ask_repos`: the same, but Claude asks you each time. A repository in both lists
  asks.
- `production_aws_profiles` and `untouchable_hosts`: older versions kept these per space.
  They still work there, and the guard joins them with the top-level lists. New ones go
  at the top.

The repository lists of every space count together: a repository listed in one space is
let through from a session in any of them.

## What Claude may change

Claude never edits this file on its own: the guard asks you first. Two tools add to it,
and only add:

- `safety_save` adds production profiles and untouchable machines.
- `backup_setup` writes a space's `backup`, only for the repository it creates in your
  GitHub account, and never moves an existing backup elsewhere.

To take anything out, edit the file yourself.

## When it cannot be read

If the file has a mistake, the program says which line. A setting it does not know is an
error too, named in the message. If the file was written by a newer version, the program
says to update instead. A file with a mistake is told in the system's language (or
`AB_LANGUAGE`), since its own `language` cannot be read. Everything else is told in the
file's `language`: an unknown setting, a newer version, a space with no `memory`, a
`default_space` that is not a space. If `language` itself is wrong, the system's.

While the file cannot be read, the guard does not know your lists. So it asks you before
every `aws`, `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync`, `sftp` and `mosh`. `augmented-brain doctor` tells you
what is wrong.

To go back to a version that worked, run `augmented-brain config history` and then
`augmented-brain config restore <number>`: both work while the file is broken. See
[Configuration versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html).

## `secrets.toml`

Next to `config.toml`, `secrets.toml` names the secrets you keep in your system
keychain, never their values:

```toml
secrets = ["telegram/alerts-bot: alerts to my phone", "smtp/newsletter: sending the newsletter"]
```

Each entry is `service/name: what it is for`. The service and the name are single words,
as the keychain knows them. Claude adds to it with the tool `secret_name_save`, and the
panel's Secrets page lists it. A value is refused. It is a file of its own because
versions before 0.6.0 refuse a setting of `config.toml` they do not know. 0.6.0 kept the
list in `config.toml` as `secrets`; `check` and the session start move it here.

## `guard.toml`

Next to `config.toml`, `guard.toml` holds what the guard never allows:

```toml
untouchable_repos = ["~/work/core", "~/work/cli-*"]
```

- `untouchable_repos`: repositories where Claude never commits, pushes or merges,
  whatever `git_allowed_repos` and `git_ask_repos` say. For the whole computer. Same form
  as those lists (`~`, a `*` in the last part, worktrees count).

The panel's Guard page writes it. If the file is missing, nothing is untouchable; if it
cannot be read, the guard asks before every commit and push. It is a file of its own for
the same reason as `secrets.toml`: versions before this one refuse a setting of
`config.toml` they do not know, and ignore a file they do not know. A session that still
runs such a version does not enforce the list. It is not carried by backups.

## `session.toml`

Next to `config.toml`, `session.toml` holds how you want your sessions:

```toml
preferred_model = "opus"
```

- `preferred_model`: the model you expect to answer (`opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku` or a full
  name such as `claude-opus-5-5`). When a session answers with another model, Claude
  tells you. It checks at the start, if Claude Code says which model it starts with. If
  not, it checks after an answer: in a new session, the second one at the latest. It
  checks again if the model changes. Once per session and model. It never changes the
  model itself: you do, with `/model` or the model picker.

The panel's Guard page writes it, and the guard asks before Claude writes it. If the file
is missing or the setting is empty, nothing is checked. It is a file of its own for the
same reason as `guard.toml`. It is not carried by backups.

## `remote.toml`

Next to `config.toml`, `remote.toml` holds the settings of [remote access](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/remote.html),
which keeps Claude reachable from another computer. `augmented-brain remote install`
creates it. It is a file of its own because versions before this one refuse a setting of
`config.toml` they do not know, and they must keep reading your configuration.

```toml
enabled = true
spaces = ["personal", "work"]
name_prefix = "my-laptop"
permission_mode = "default"
folders = { work = "~/code/clients" }
```

All are optional:

- `enabled`: whether remote access is set up. `remote install` writes `true` and
  `remote uninstall` writes `false`. Only when it is `true` does `doctor` check the
  services; a file it cannot read is a warning either way.
- `spaces`: the spaces that get a session, each in a service of its own. Default: the
  `default_space`, or the only space when there is one.
- `name_prefix`: sessions are called `<name_prefix>-<space>`, such as `my-laptop-personal`.
  One plain word: letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore. Default: the computer's name.
- `permission_mode`: how much Claude may do without asking. One of `default`,
  `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk` and `bypassPermissions`. Default: `default`,
  where Claude asks as usual and the guard stays in force. **Do not use
  `bypassPermissions`**: it lets whoever connects run anything, with no questions, and
  leaves the computer open.
- `folders`: where a space's session starts, when it is not the space's first work folder
  (the default). The folder must exist and lie inside a work folder of that space, so the
  session still loads that space.

Run `augmented-brain remote install` again after changing it, so the services pick it up.

## Other files in the folder

- `profile.md`: your profile, for every space.
- `shared/`: the shared notes (rules, references and lessons for every space).
- `state/`: what this computer knows of each space's sessions. Never backed up.
- `migrations/`: a full copy of notes before a new version moved them.
- `panel.json` and `panel.lock`: where the panel listens while it runs, and its lock.
  The guard never lets Claude read `panel.json`: it holds the panel's key.
- `remote/<space>/`: the folder where the remote access service of a space starts, only for
  a space with no work folder of its own. It is made a work folder of that space.
- `review-<space>.draft`: a weekly review started in the panel and not finished yet.
- `history/`: the last 10 versions of your configuration, with who changed them. Only on
  this computer, never backed up. See [Configuration versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html).

## Environment variables

Set these in your shell to change how the program behaves:

- `AB_CONFIG_DIR`: use this folder as the configuration folder.
- `AB_LANGUAGE`: `en` or `es`, the language before there is a configuration, or while it
  cannot be read (the installer and `init` use it).
- `AB_NO_AUTO_BACKUP=1`: do not back up when a session ends.
- `AB_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`: do not ask GitHub, once a day, whether there is a new version.
- `AB_NO_BROWSER=1`: `augmented-brain panel` prints the address instead of opening the
  browser.

The installer reads a few more:

- `AB_YES=1`: answer yes to every question.
- `AB_NO_DESKTOP=1`: do not offer the Claude desktop app.
- `AB_DESKTOP_TIMEOUT`: on Linux, how many seconds the desktop app's download may take
  before the installer gives up and goes on without it. Default 480 (8 minutes).
- `AB_INSTALL_DIR`: where to put the program. Default `~/.local/bin`.
- `AB_NO_INIT=1`: only install the program, without setting anything up.
- `AB_VERSION`, `AB_RELEASE_URL`, `AB_API_URL`, `AB_RETRY_DELAY`, `AB_MARKETPLACE` and
  `AB_DESKTOP_URL`: for testing: which version, where the release files are, the GitHub
  API to fall back on, the wait between tries, a folder or repository to take the plugin
  from instead of the one inside the program, and where the desktop app's apt repository
  is. `augmented-brain update` ignores them all: for its tests it takes `--from`.
- `AB_ALLOW_ROOT=1`: on Linux and macOS, install even as root (`sudo`). Without it the
  installer refuses: it needs no root, and as root the program and its settings would
  end up belonging to root, or in root's home, not yours.

## Claude Code's own settings

One setting of Claude Code matters here. If Claude Code keeps a memory of its own for your
spaces' folders, it drifts from the space's. `augmented-brain doctor` tells you, and the
fix is `"autoMemoryEnabled": false` in Claude Code's settings, in the file `doctor`
names.

The full format of every file is in the [memory format](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html).


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html

# Memory format

**Status: format version 1** (see "Format version" below). This document defines how augmented brain stores what you and your assistant know: what files exist, what goes in each, and which fields the program reads. Everything is plain Markdown that you can open, edit and search with any tool.

## Principles

1. **Plain files, yours.** One folder of Markdown per space. No database, no hosted service.
2. **The program reads fields, never prose.** Anything the program needs (a task's status, who it waits on, its next step) lives in the file's header. The body is free text, in any language.
3. **Indexes are generated.** You never edit an index by hand; the program rebuilds it after every change. Hand-kept indexes drift.
4. **Nothing is deleted.** Closed tasks stay, marked closed. What is no longer needed day to day can go to `archive/`, which is never loaded.
5. **Short at the top, detail below.** The file loaded at the start of every session stays small; detail lives one link away.

## Spaces

A **space** keeps one part of your life apart from the others, for example `work` and `personal`. Each space has:

- its own memory folder (everything below);
- its own rules, on top of the common ones;
- its own backup repository.

The space is chosen by **the folder you open the assistant in**. Spaces never read each other's memory. They share the program, the common rules, the shared notes (below), the safety hooks and the risk settings (which cloud profiles are production, which hosts must not be touched): those are for the whole machine, so a production profile saved from one space is guarded in all of them.

Spaces are declared in the configuration file (see "Configuration" below), not inside the memory.

By default, `augmented-brain init` creates two spaces, `work` and `personal` (in Spanish, `trabajo` and `personal`). Each one is a folder in `~/augmented-brain/`, which is its work folder, and its memory folder sits inside it as `notes/` (`notas/`). Any other layout can be set with `init --custom` or by editing the configuration.

A session that runs outside every work folder (for example, the scratch folder the Claude desktop app opens a new session in) uses the **default space**, `default_space` in the configuration; `init` sets it to `personal`, and `space add` sets it when there are two spaces or more and none is set (to `personal` if a space has that name, or else to the first space). Its backup is the one that carries the profile. Without one, no memory is loaded there and the assistant tells the user which folders to open.

## Layout of a space

```
<memory folder>/
├── MEMORY.md          # the index loaded at the start of every session (generated)
├── profile.md         # optional: what only applies in this space (your role at work…)
├── inbox.md           # quick captures, processed in the weekly review
├── areas/             # ongoing responsibilities (one file each)
├── tasks/             # projects with a beginning and an end (one file each)
├── knowledge/         # how things work (reference) and what you learned (lesson)
├── people/            # who the user deals with, so a first name finds the right person
├── rules/             # this space's own rules (the common rules ship with the program; shared ones live in the configuration folder)
├── reviews/           # one file per weekly review
├── docs/              # optional: long documents of a task (plans, analyses, reports); never loaded
│   └── <task>/
└── archive/           # old journals (journals/), merged files; never loaded, never deleted
    └── sessions/      # summaries Claude Code wrote when it compacted a conversation
```

`docs/` keeps the long documents a task produces, so they stay with the notes and out of the repositories the work touches (a repository only gets what its team needs). Each one sits under the id of its task, is plain Markdown or any other file, has no header, and is linked from the task. The program does not read it.

A summary in `archive/sessions/` is plain Markdown with no header, named `<date>-<time>-<session>.md`; the program writes it, with any secret taken out, and adds a journal line to the session's active task pointing at it.

`MEMORY.md` is the index the session start hands the assistant, a little shorter: each live task goes without its summary, and with its next step (its first 120 characters) only when it waits on you (the assistant reads a task before working on it), and without the list of rules, which the start gives whole. It comes in up to three parts of the start (see "Rules"). An index too long for them is cut, and the assistant is told where to read it whole.

**Your profile** (who you are, your language, how you like answers) is the same person in every space, so it lives once, next to the configuration: `profile.md` in the configuration folder. A space's own `profile.md` only adds what applies there.

The shared profile has two sections the program knows by their headings, in English or
Spanish: the first ("About me" / "Sobre mí", with the name line) and the work style
("How I like to work" / "Cómo me gusta trabajar"). Other sections a person adds by hand
are kept: the program reads them as part of the first one.

**Shared notes** are the rules, references and lessons that hold in every space (how git
behaves, how the person likes answers). They live once, next to the configuration, in
`shared/` inside the configuration folder, laid out like a space but with only
`rules/` and `knowledge/` (plus the generated `MEMORY.md` and `.augmented-brain/format`).
A shared note has no area, since areas belong to one space; a task, area, person or
review there is a problem, reported and left out. Every space sees them: a note of a
space may name a shared note in `related`, and the session start loads the shared rules
like the space's (see Rules) and lists the shared references and lessons, by title and file. A shared note never links into a
space. They are migrated like a space's notes, and kept in the backup of the default
space, under `.augmented-brain/shared/`, like the profile.

## File header

Every file except `MEMORY.md`, `inbox.md` and what is in `docs/` and `archive/` starts with a YAML header between `---` lines (a byte order mark before it is fine). Keys and enumerated values are always English, whatever language you write in.

```yaml
---
id: task-backup-restore          # unique in the space; also the file name without .md
type: task                       # profile | area | task | reference | lesson | rule | person | review
title: Backup and restore        # shown in indexes; any language
summary: One line on what it is  # shown in indexes; any language
area: area-platform              # tasks, references and lessons: the area they belong to
repos: [infra/terraform]         # optional: repositories it touches, relative to the space's work folder
related: [lesson-git-filters]    # optional: other ids; the program keeps links two-way
created: 2026-10-15
updated: 2026-10-15
---
```

A repository in `repos:` that is in none of the space's work folders (it was moved,
renamed or deleted, or this computer never had it) is reported, never fixed by itself:
`augmented-brain check` and the panel's Health page list them, and reading the task
tells the assistant to ask the user where it is now. A closed task is not checked. An
absolute path, or one starting with `~`, is taken as it is.

Every field of the header holds one line. A line break in one, or any other control
character (tabs, the Unicode line and paragraph separators), is read as a space, and
spaces in a row as one: a title, summary, status, `waiting_on`, next step or watch
date written over several lines by hand still makes one line in `MEMORY.md` and at the
session start, so no field can open a section there. Only `repos` and `related` keep
their spaces, since they name paths and ids. The program writes them that way too, and
refuses a field longer than its limit, counted in characters, when it changes: title
300, summary 1,000, next step 2,000, `waiting_on` 200, a watch date's `what` 1,000. A
journal entry may be up to 32,000 characters, a capture 4,000, a note 512,000 and the
profile 64,000; the error says where the longer text goes (a file under `docs/<task>/`,
which the journal names). A journal entry of several lines keeps them, each one after
the first indented, so it stays one entry and never starts a heading or a step.

Dates (`created`, `updated`, and each `watch` date of a task) are `YYYY-MM-DD`. One
written another way (`2026-11-3`) keeps the note, but is reported until fixed, since it
would never come up.

A file whose name starts with `.` is not a note and is never read (an editor's lock
file, such as Emacs's `.#task-x.md`). A file or folder that cannot be read (its
permissions, a broken link) is reported and left out; the rest of the space loads as
usual. So is a folder of a type of note (`tasks/`, `knowledge/`…) that is a link to
another place: its notes are not read, so put the folder itself there.

### Task fields

Tasks add the fields that drive the whole workflow:

```yaml
status: plan                     # see "Task lifecycle"
waiting_on: me                   # me | nobody | a person's name | another task id
next: Approve the plan           # the single next action, one line
watch:                           # optional: dates to look at something again
  - date: 2026-11-16
    what: Certificates renewed?
    done: false
```

A watch date that is not `done` and falls in the next 7 days, or is already past, is
brought up at the start of the session. This holds for closed tasks too: closing is when
the checks for later are written down, so they come up until they are marked `done`.

### Subtasks

A task may be part of a bigger one, with one more field:

```yaml
parent: task-new-website         # optional: the id of the task this one is a part of
```

A subtask is a whole task (its own status, waiting_on, next step and journal). Make one
for a part that waits on someone else or goes at its own pace; anything smaller is a
step (below). The rules:

- The parent is an existing task that is not itself a subtask: one level only. The
  program refuses to open a subtask under a missing task, a note that is not a task, a
  subtask, or a closed task.
- A parent cannot be closed while any of its subtasks is not closed. Parking the parent
  leaves its subtasks as they are.
- The index lists a live subtask under its parent, indented. A subtask whose parent is
  closed, someday or missing is listed on its own, so it is never hidden. A `parent`
  that does not exist, is not a task, is the task itself or is itself a subtask is
  reported as a problem (like an `area` that does not exist), and so is a `parent` on a
  note that is not a task; the note is still read and can still be written, and is
  listed on its own, once.

### Steps

A step is a Markdown checkbox in the task's **Plan** section, the level-2 heading
`## Plan` (numbered or not, `## 3. Plan`, any case):

```markdown
## 3. Plan
- [x] Buy the domain
- [ ] Point it to the server
```

Steps need no field: the program finds the Plan heading and reads its checkboxes
(`- [ ]` or `- [x]`, also with `*`), outside code blocks, numbered from 1 in order. The
index and `pending` show how many are done ("1/2 steps") when there are any. Adding a
step puts it, unticked, at the end of the Plan; ticking or unticking one changes only its
`[ ]`, and writes one line in the journal.

## Task lifecycle

A task moves through six phases. You approve each change of phase; inside a phase the assistant works without asking at every step.

| `status` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `definition` | What we want, what is out, and how we will know it worked |
| `analysis` | How things really are, measured, not assumed |
| `plan` | Ordered steps, each with how to undo it |
| `execution` | Doing it, writing a journal entry as we go |
| `validation` | Proving the "done" criterion |
| `closed` | Finished; the closing checklist is done |

Two more statuses pause a task without losing anything:

| `status` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parked` | Paused, resumed soon; `next` says exactly how |
| `someday` | Not for weeks; leaves the session index, stays in its area |

Skipping phases is allowed, and seen: the journal line of the change names the phases
skipped (`Status: definition → execution, skipping analysis, plan.`). A closed task is
never closed again, so its result is not written over. It opens again only with a
reason, which goes to the journal (`Reopened (now plan): …`).

### Task body

The body uses these sections, in your language (the templates write the headings for you):

1. **Essentials**: three to six lines that are enough to resume the task without reading anything else. Rewritten every time the task is parked.
2. **Definition**, **Analysis**, **Plan**, **Validation**, **Closing**: one per phase.
3. **Journal**: dated lines, `- YYYY-MM-DD — what happened`. Always the last section.

The program never searches the prose. It relies on two positions only: the essentials are the **first** section, and the journal is the **last**, so a new entry is simply appended at the end of the file. The one exception is the checkboxes of the Plan section (see "Steps"). The other is a long journal: when a task note passes 24 KB, the program moves its oldest entries (a dated line and the lines under it, up to the next dated line), as they were, to `archive/journals/<task id>-<first date>-<last date>.md`, keeping about the last 8 KB of entries in the note, and never fewer than 4 KB moved at once. In their place it writes one dated line, dated as the last entry moved so the journal stays in date order, that names that file; the line is recognized by the path `archive/journals/….md` in it, whatever the language. The file is plain Markdown with no header: a title, a line on where the entries came from, then the entries. It is written before the note, so a failure leaves a copy too many, never one too few. Anything above the first dated line of the journal stays.

## Areas

An area is something you look after with no end date (your platform, your observability, your side project). Its body says what you look after, how it is going and what to watch. The program lists its tasks and knowledge in the area automatically, from their `area` field.

## Knowledge

- **reference**: how something works (a system, a deployment, a tool).
- **lesson**: something learned, with a title that already states the conclusion.

Both belong to an area and can relate to tasks.

## People

A person is someone the user deals with: `people/person-<name>.md`. The title is the name,
and the summary says who they are to the user and the other names the user calls them
("my manager · also: Marcos"), so the index alone tells the assistant who "Marcos" is. The
body keeps anything else worth remembering. People belong to a space: work contacts stay
in the work space. The panel reads the role and the other names back from the summary
when it changes a person; the name (title and id) stays.

## Repositories

What each of the user's git repositories is lives in one reference of the space,
`knowledge/ref-repositories.md` (`type: reference`, no area), so it is backed up with
the notes. It is an ordinary reference: releases that know nothing of it read it as
one, and it needs no new field. Its body has one line per repository:

```
- `~/code/website` — The public website, built with Hugo
```

The path is written with `~` when it is under the home folder (otherwise absolute), or,
by hand, relative to a work folder of the space, as `repos:` writes it. The text after
the dash (` — `, or ` - ` by hand) is one line of plain text, at most 300 characters,
and may not hold a secret. Any other line (a paragraph of your own, a heading) is left
alone. The panel's Repositories page and the MCP tool `repo_describe` write it, only for
folders inside the space's work folders: a new description replaces the line of that
repository, and an empty one takes it out. The note is made the first time.

## Inbox

`inbox.md` has no header. Each capture is one line, with the date it was captured:

```
- 2026-10-17 — Look at the new CI runner
- 2026-10-17 — Call the insurance (remind: 2026-10-22)
```

A capture ending in `(remind: YYYY-MM-DD)` is brought up at the start of the session from
7 days before that date, and every day after it, until the capture is processed (in the
weekly review, or marked as dealt with). Any other line (the heading, a paragraph) is left alone.

The text of a capture is one line, read as a header field is (above). Its endings
`(remind: YYYY-MM-DD)` and `(from <space>)` are marks only the program writes: typed
as part of the text, they are kept between square brackets instead
(`[from personal]`), so a capture made here never passes for one another space sent.
The same holds for `(from <space>)` at the end of a journal entry.

## Reviews

The weekly review goes through the inbox (each capture becomes a task, goes to an area or
knowledge, or is dropped), the live tasks untouched for 14 days or more, and the dates due
in the coming week. Processed captures leave the inbox, and the review is kept as
`reviews/review-<date>.md` (`type: review`), with what was decided as its body and the
first line as its summary; the captures it took out of the inbox follow, as dated lines
under a heading of their own. The review is saved first: one that cannot be saved takes
nothing out of the inbox. When the last review is 7 days old or more and there is
something to go through, the session start offers a new one. A review done in the
panel keeps one line per decision while it goes on in a draft on this machine
(`review-<space>.draft` in the configuration folder, never in the notes), and writes
those lines into the review's body when it is finished.

## Rules

Rules tell the assistant how to work. There are three levels:

- **common rules**, shipped with the program (answer style, verify before advising, never commit or push unless asked, never escalate to root, never write secrets…);
- **shared rules**, the person's own for every space, in the shared notes (for example, "answer in short sentences, one idea each");
- **space rules**, in `rules/`, for what only applies to that space (for example, "hosts db01–db03 are never restarted without explicit permission").

All of them are loaded at the start of every session, whole. The start comes in up to
nine parts, each of about 9,500 characters at most: the heading with the profile, the
index (up to three parts), the common rules in a part of their own, so nothing else can
push them out, and the shared and space rules in the parts left. Only the parts that have
something are sent, and they are counted that way ("part 2 of 3"). A
rule's section titled `History` (or `Historia`) stays in its file: it tells how the rule
came to be, not what to do. A rule that does not fit whole goes as one line, its title
and summary, with the path of its file; so a rule's summary should say what to do.

## Format version

The notes of each space say which version of this format they follow, in
`.augmented-brain/format` inside the memory folder: one line with a number. The
configuration folder says its own, for the configuration and the profile, as
`format = N` at the top of `config.toml`. Neither saying it means version 1, which is
also never written to `config.toml`, because releases from before versions were
written refuse settings they do not know. This document describes version 1.

When a release writes something in a new way, it raises the version and brings a step
that moves version N to N+1. At the start of a session (and in `augmented-brain check`)
the program copies the whole folder to `migrations/` in the configuration folder, runs
the missing steps one at a time and writes the new version after each, so a step that
stops half way runs again from there. The copy goes in a folder of its own, symbolic
links copied as links, and holds a file `.copy-complete` once all of it is on the disk;
a run again from the same version keeps that copy and makes no other, so it never holds
notes half moved. Notes of a newer version than the program knows are never written: the
program asks to be updated.

Every note is replaced in one step: written to a temporary file next to it
(`<name>.<digits>.tmp`), synced to the disk, renamed over the note, and its folder
synced, so a power cut leaves the old note or the new one, never an empty one. A
temporary file left by a write cut short is removed at the start of a session once it
is an hour old. A note that is a symbolic link is never written through: the write is
refused (the configuration folder may hold links, for people who keep it in a
repository of their own).

## Generated files

The program rebuilds these after every change; editing them by hand is pointless:

- `MEMORY.md`: your profile line, the rules, the areas, and the live tasks grouped by area, one line each, with status, steps done when the Plan has any, who it waits on and the next step; subtasks indented under their parent.
- The "Tasks" and "Knowledge" lists inside each area.

## Configuration

`~/.config/augmented-brain/config.toml` (or the platform equivalent) declares the spaces:

```toml
language = "en"                  # en | es: the language the program speaks to you
default_space = "personal"       # used outside every work folder (optional)
production_aws_profiles = ["prod", "prod-eu"]   # every space: the user confirms first
untouchable_hosts = ["db01", "db02", "db03"]    # ssh, scp, rsync, sftp, mosh to them: the user confirms first
root_ask = ["db01 until 2026-10-31"]            # root there asks instead of being refused, until then

[spaces.work]
memory = "~/augmented-brain/work/notes"
work_folders = ["~/augmented-brain/work", "~/code"]   # opening the assistant here selects this space
backup = "git@github.com:me/brain-work-private.git"
git_allowed_repos = ["~/code/website", "~/code/website-*"]   # the assistant may commit and push here, with git -C
git_ask_repos = ["~/code/infra"]                # the same, once the user confirms each time

[spaces.personal]
memory = "~/augmented-brain/personal/notes"
work_folders = ["~/augmented-brain/personal"]
backup = "git@github.com:me/brain-personal-private.git"
```

In `git_allowed_repos` and `git_ask_repos` the last part of a path may hold a `*`, which
matches one folder (`~/code/website-*` is every `website-<name>` next to `website`), and a
git worktree of a listed repository counts as that repository, wherever it is. The guard
joins the lists of every space, as it does with the production profiles: a repository
belongs to the person, not to the space a session runs in. A repository in both lists
asks. Even in an allowed one, a push that rewrites or deletes on the remote (a force, a
delete, a mirror, or a refspec starting with `+` or `:`) asks.

The same lists decide on merging a pull request (`gh pr merge`, `glab mr merge`, `glab mr
accept`), which pushes to the branch it goes into. As a push counts only a repository
written with `git -C`, a merge counts only a repository the command names. One way is a
`cd` before it (`cd <repo> && gh pr merge 12`). The other, in the session's own folder,
is `-R`/`--repo` or the pull request's address, when that is one of the folder's
remotes: Claude Code drops a `cd` to the folder the session is already in. Never the
session's folder alone, nor `GH_REPO`, which a command may inherit unseen. The folder
must be the listed folder itself or a worktree of it, not a folder inside it. A
repository the command
names (`-R`/`--repo`, `GH_REPO`, `GITLAB_REPO`, the pull request's address) must be one
of that repository's remotes, read from its `.git/config` (includes are not followed); a
name with no host is on `github.com` or `gitlab.com` (or `GH_HOST`, `GITLAB_HOST`).
`gh pr merge --admin` always asks. Publishing a release stays for the user.

`production_aws_profiles` and `untouchable_hosts` may also appear inside a space, as older
versions wrote them: the guard applies the top-level lists and every space's together.
Host names match ignoring case, and a short name matches the full one either way (`db01`
and `db01.example.com`).

`root_ask` holds temporary exceptions for root, one machine each: `"<host> until <date>"`.
The date is a day (the exception lasts to its end, in UTC) or a time
(`2026-10-31T23:59Z`), and it is required, so no exception is left behind. While it
lasts, a command that would run as root on that machine (`sudo`, `su`, also inside
`ssh <host> '…'`) asks the user instead of being refused; the command it runs is still
checked. The host is matched as ssh names it, or against this machine's name. After the
date the entry does nothing, and `augmented-brain doctor` says it can be removed. The
session start tells the assistant which exceptions are in force, and names those that
cannot be read (they grant nothing); `doctor` names those too.

`secrets.toml`, next to `config.toml`, names the secrets the user keeps in the system
keychain: `secrets = ["<service>/<name>: what it is for", …]`. It is a file of its own,
not a setting of `config.toml`, because programs before 0.6.0 refuse a setting they do
not know; 0.6.0 kept the list in `config.toml`, and 0.6.1 moves it here at the start of
a session or with `check`. The service and the name are single words (letters, digits,
`. _ @ + -`, not starting with `-`), and what it is for is one line of plain text (no
quotes, backslashes or control characters), as the keychain knows them (`secret-tool` attributes `service` and
`name` on Linux; a generic password's service and account on macOS). It never holds a
value: anything that looks like one is refused. It is the same list in every space. The
assistant adds to it with the MCP tool `secret_name_save` (saving a listed name changes
what it is for); the panel lists it, adds and removes names, says which tasks name each
one, and, only when asked, whether this computer's keychain has it. An entry that cannot
be read is left out and counted on the panel's page.

Three more files sit next to `config.toml`. None of them goes into a backup.

- `guard.toml` holds `untouchable_repos`: repositories where the assistant never commits,
  pushes or merges, whatever the other lists say, for the whole machine. Same form as
  `git_allowed_repos`. A missing file means nothing is untouchable.
- `session.toml` holds `preferred_model`: the model the user expects to answer (`opus`,
  or a full name). When a session answers with another one, the assistant tells the
  user. Empty or missing: nothing is checked.
- `remote.toml` holds the settings of remote access: `enabled`, `spaces`, `name_prefix`,
  `permission_mode` and `folders`.

They are files of their own because earlier programs refuse a setting of `config.toml`
they do not know. Every change of `config.toml`, `guard.toml`, `remote.toml`,
`session.toml`, `profile.md` or `secrets.toml` is kept as a version in `history/` in the
configuration folder, with who made it. The last 10 are kept, only on this machine, never
in a backup. The user's guide has every setting:
[Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html) and
[Configuration versions](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/config-history.html).

## Backup

Each space backs up to its own private git repository: the memory folder itself is the
repository. Every backup also copies this space's part of the configuration into
`.augmented-brain/` inside the memory folder, so restoring on a new machine needs nothing
else. The default space's backup (or the only space's) also carries the profile and
`secrets.toml`, and says `default_space` in its copy of the configuration, so a restore
makes it the default space again when the machine has none, and brings the secrets'
names when the machine has none (also from a 0.6.0 backup, which kept them in its copy
of the configuration), then names those this machine's keychain lacks; no other backup does, so the personal profile
never reaches a work repository. The
machine-wide guard lists are in no backup (they may name work machines): after a restore
that leaves them empty, `restore` and `doctor` say so, and the next session offers to ask for them
again. A restore never brings `git_allowed_repos` or `git_ask_repos` either, since someone
else may have changed the backup: they are given again on the new machine. A backup that
holds a symbolic link is never restored, nor merged with another machine's, since
augmented brain never writes one. Notes are written readable by their owner only (files
0600, folders 0700); a restore makes the restored notes so, `augmented-brain check` fixes
a space whose notes others could read, and `augmented-brain doctor` warns about it. Paths are kept with `~`, so they point to the new machine's home, and
the notes go back to the same place inside the work folder. A restore also installs the
Claude Code plugin when it is missing.

A backup is refused while any file of the memory holds a secret (the made-up keys of
AWS's documentation are not secrets). The tools refuse to write one in the first place:
a note may not hold more secrets than its old version did, so a note that already holds
one (as an import may leave it) can still be changed to take it out. Files over 50 MB are left out, and the user is told.
The repository gets a `.gitattributes` (`inbox.md merge=union`: captures from two machines
are both kept, so one processed on one machine may come back if the other captured at the
same time) and a `.gitignore` (`*.tmp`, `.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, `desktop.ini`); lines
the user adds to them stay. The generated index is rebuilt after a restore.

When another machine changed the same notes, the backup merges before pushing. A note
that each machine changed only by adding journal entries (dated lines) and moving its
`updated` date is joined by itself: every entry either added, in date order, and the
later date. So is a task where one machine moved old entries to `archive/journals/`:
each line that names such a file is replaced by the file's entries to compare, and put
back once joined. An earlier program, which does not do this, stops there as with any
other conflict. Any other conflict stops the backup without pushing, naming the notes to
merge by hand.

Each git call of a backup or restore stops after 3 minutes without an answer (over
https, also on a transfer slower than 1 KB a second for a minute), and a backup waits at
most 10 minutes for another one to finish; both say why.

## State of this machine

`state/<space>.json` in the configuration folder keeps, for this machine only (never
backed up, no text of the conversation): the sessions that started and ended, with the
path of Claude Code's transcript of each, the Claude process each runs in, and each
one's active task, when it was last written and when the assistant was last reminded to
write. Earlier versions kept a single active task for the whole space; it is no longer
read. The Stop reminder, the request after a
compaction and the offer to recover a session that did not end come from it.

`state/guard.seal` keeps a fingerprint of the guard's lists as the user last accepted
them: at a session start, or when the panel saved them. While the lists differ from it, a
commit, push or merge they allow asks first. `history/` keeps the last 10 versions of the
configuration (see Configuration).

`panel.json`, also in the configuration folder and readable only by the user, says where
the panel listens while it runs (its process, port and key); it goes away when the panel
stops. `panel.lock`, next to it, lets one `augmented-brain panel` (or `panel stop`) at a
time start or stop the panel, so several at once start only one. The panel changes notes
only through the same code as the MCP tools.

## Decisions

- **A folder per type**, not one flat folder with prefixes: a newcomer sees at a glance what there is and where each thing goes.
- **One profile for the person**, next to the configuration; each space may add its own `profile.md`.
- **Shared notes, not spaces that read each other.** What holds everywhere lives once, in the shared notes, rather than copied into each space (copies drift) or by letting a space read another's memory (which would mix work and personal). Only rules and knowledge can be shared; tasks, areas and people stay in their space.
- **Importing an existing memory** of Claude Code (`augmented-brain import`) reads the header only: a field this format has is kept, at the top or under `metadata`; a person's own conventions are turned into those fields by a step of their own before importing, not by the program. It plans first and writes only with `--apply`, never over an existing note, and never changes the source.


---

Source: https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/compatibility.html

# What stays stable


augmented brain numbers its versions the usual way: **1.x** means every version that
starts with 1. From 1.0 on, nothing on this page breaks inside 1.x. If something here
ever has to break, that is version **2.0**, and the changelog says what changes and how
to move.

The beta versions (0.x) already follow these rules, but they are not a promise yet.

## What is promised

- **Your notes.** The format the [memory format](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/memory-format.html) describes:
  the folders, the types of note, the fields of the header and what each one means. When
  a 1.x writes something in a new way, it brings the step that moves your notes forward,
  and runs it by itself after a full copy. Notes of any beta (0.x) move forward the same
  way.
- **Your configuration.** `config.toml`, `secrets.toml`, `guard.toml`, `session.toml`,
  `remote.toml` and `profile.md`: every setting in the
  [configuration reference](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html) keeps its name and what it does.
- **The commands.** Every command and option in the [command reference](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/commands.html)
  stays and does the same. So do the exit codes that page gives (for example, `watch pr`
  ends with 0 or 1).
- **The assistant's tools.** Every MCP tool in the [tool reference](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/mcp-tools.html) keeps
  its name, its parameters and what it does. A version may add tools, or parameters you
  can leave out; never a new parameter a call must give. This matters because your rules
  and notes name these tools.
- **The environment variables** in [Configuration](https://icalvete.github.io/augmented-brain/guide/configuration.html#environment-variables)
  (`AB_CONFIG_DIR`, `AB_LANGUAGE`, `AB_NO_AUTO_BACKUP`…) and those of the installer.
- **Backups.** A backup made with any 1.x restores with any later 1.x.
- **Installing and updating.** The install line on the front page keeps working, and
  `augmented-brain update` takes any 1.x to the latest one.

**A name that changes keeps working.** When a command, an option, a setting, a tool or a
parameter gets a new name, the old one still works until 2.0 and says what replaced it.
Nothing on the list goes away inside 1.x.

**An earlier version never damages your notes.** With two computers, or with a session
still open after an update, an older program may read notes a newer one wrote. The two
versions before the newest read them; if the format changed, they refuse them and ask
you to update, without writing anything.

## What is not promised

- **The words.** The program's messages, what the tools answer, what the assistant
  reads when a session starts, and the wording of the common rules change to explain
  things better. Do not read them from a script; use the exit codes.
- **The panel.** Its pages, how they look and their addresses.
- **The inside.** The folders `state/`, `history/`, `migrations/` and `marketplace/` of
  the configuration folder, the hidden commands (`panel serve`, `remote watch`), what
  `hook` and `mcp` print (the names stay: the plugin calls them), and the Go code (it is
  not a library).
- **What the guard lets through.** It may get stricter in any version: a command that
  passes today may ask tomorrow. Your lists (`git_allowed_repos` and the rest) keep
  working.
